Mr. BUCK CLAYTON
REELS I AND II
INTERVIEWED BY
MR. STANLEY DANCE
Buck, would you like to begin with where you were born and how things were in the town where you were born?

Yes. I was born in Parsons, Kansas. It's a small town in South East Kansas about 150 miles from Kansas City, Missouri. I was born November 12, 1911. And I went to school there and I began my first musical studies when I was six years old. I was learning piano and I studied piano until I was 18 years old.
Well, were your parents musically inclined?

Yes, but not professionally. You see, my father, earlier in his life has played cornet and my mother had played piano, but nothing professional. They were quite active in social groups and church affairs and things like that.
Well your father was a minister wasn't he?
Yes, he was a minister later, later in his life.
Oh, I see.
And my mother had a beauty parlour. She had a beauty parlour.
Well how big a town was Parsons?
At that time, Parsons was about 11 or 12,000 people. I don't know what it is today, now.
Well what made Parsons tick?

Well at that time the railroads. It was a railroad center. There was the MK&T, Missouri, Kansas and Texas line. The Frisco line and the whole town centered on the railroads. But right now all of the railroads are gone from Parsons. It's a different town now.
Well what did the, I mean why did the, what did the railroads do there, that was a junction, I mean....
That was a junction, yes.
They didn't bring cattle there.
No, just through, you know coming from Texas to Kansas City, you had to
come through my,..and we also had big railroad yards there that kept everybody working, for years. My father worked on the railroad too at one time.
Oh really?
Yes.
Well how did he sort of come to make religion his thing?

I don't really know. Unless it was, you see he used to sing in the choir as a bass singer and my dad was a, he was a church going man, and he was quite active in all the church, so both was my mother. Yes, my mother. They/were active, very active in musical work, church music.
Well in those days would the church represent a more important position in the lives of colored people than it does today?
Yes. Yes I think so.
I mean, that was, there was a social aspect to that as well.

Right, right. Much more than it is now. I remember my mother, you see my family was Methodist and the other church was Baptist naturally. So we were always in a little battle between the Methodists and the Baptists. But everybody at that time and being a small town too,
we all from the time we were three or four years old, we had to go to Sunday School and put a nickel or a dime in the collection box which kids don't do much now.
So, my mother was a choir leader. My father was the bass, the best bass singer, we had two or three. He was the best bass. And you know Wild Bill Davis the organ player?
Yes.
His father was one of the baritones there, singer, I mean.
Singer.
And his father and my father had a beautiful quartet of singers.
Oh really?
My dad sang bass. His dad sang baritone and they had two tenors. They used to win prizes.
What would they, they would sing sort of gospel or spiritual things?
Right.
Oh, that's interesting. Did you know Wild Bill Davis ?
Oh yes, sure.
In those days? You're about the same age, huh?
No, I was older than he was.
Oh. You were.

He was born I believe on the same street that I was born on in Kansas, Parsons, called Grand Avenue. In fact, he was born about three blocks from me, but he was just one of three or four brothers at that time. I didn't know anything about him playing music until I came back from Shang Hai, China and I went home to visit my mother. And in my house was all of the young, aspiring, young musicians wanted to meet me, Sir Charles was one.
Charles Thompson?
Yes. /Charles, Wild Bill. They are the only two that you know of. Then there were a lot of them there that......
But of course your two or three years difference at that age is a very big thing isn't it?
Oh sure it is. Sure it is, yes. Actually I'm five years older than Sir Charles, but they both were beginners at that time. And
Wild Bill and Sir Charles came by my house one Sunday afternoon and played all night, all day rather.
They were both playing piano?
Yes.
Well, oh you learned to play piano first?
Yes.
You told me once that your father played tuba.

He did when I, when, as he got older. He gradually got away from that cornet and when I was learning trumpet, which he taught me, the scales, but I already knew how to read from playing piano. And we had a chapel orchestra that played for churches, funerals and social affairs in the park on Sunday afternoons and we rehearsed at my house, every Sunday. And my dad played tuba then.

Me and, there were three trumpets and my father was on the bass at that time. You see, but earlier during the years like when King Oliver was in New Orleans, my dad was in Texas playing trumpet, cornet, rather.
Well was he sort of playing in the equivalent of jazz orchestras at that time?
Yes, a little bit.
He was?
But not when I knew him. I mean that was before I was born. You see, my dad was playing at the same time King Oliver was playing.
Well what sort of bands, were there any that you ever heard of?
No.
Big names?
No. You see, Texas was a little, wasn't New Orleans. Everything was centered around New Orleans. But there were always good musicians in Texas, you see.
Now, well in this chapel orchestra, did your father do the teaching or who taught the players then?
We didn't have to teach them. They all, they all knew.
Oh, they were all musicians, oh I see. They were church goers who .....
Who knew how to play. We had
French Horn players. We had a wonderful pianist who is in New York right now, Noreen Tate.
No relation to Buddy Tate?
No. No relation.
That's NOREEN?
NORENE.
Oh, ENE.
Yes, Norene Tate. She was a wonderful pianist. She played down in the village for quite a few years.
Well you mean as a jazz pianist?

Yes. Oh she was, she and I were both the only young people in the band. We used to hit a jazz note when sometimes we'd be playing a church song and old dad would turn around and say, don't do that son, don't do that. That doesn't belong in here. If it had a jazz note in it.
The church people were quick to recognise jazz, huh? Now there's just one thing about the church. Wasn't Sir Charles Thompson's father ......
His father was a minister.
What religion was he, I mean what......
I never knew.
I mean what denomination?
I never did know. But he was
He was a minister in Parsons?
No he was a minister about twenty miles from Parsons. A Town called Independence.
But didn't they live in Parsons?
No.
Oh, they didn't.
Sir Charles lived there but I don't know if his father did. I'll have to ask about.
Well that's not important, but
Yes, because I remember it was Parsons that some guys sneaked in the window and Sir Charles sneaked out of the window and ran away with his band from Omaha, from Nebraska.
Oh really?
Yes. They got him out.
Well when did you, after, I take it this chapel orchestra was good experience for you.
It was.
Now when did you sort of begin to play as a, well more or less when did you begin to play jazz?

Jazz? Well I started in Parsons. But one time there was a band that came to my home that their trumpet player had got sick on the way there and he couldn't play. It was only about a five-piece band. And they had to play this dance. And they would have given anything to find a trumpet player. And I'd been playing trumpet about three or four months.
So they hired me because I was the only one they could find, but I only knew, my repertoire was about four songs.
(Do you remember what they were?)
'Sweet Sue,' 'Hard to Get Gertie,' 'Dinah' and something else. So we played at the dance that night, we played those four songs over and over and over again.
At different tempos?
Right. 'Dinah,' gee, we played 'Dinah' so much. And I got five dollars for my first gig
The fourth song that I couldn't remember was, "Deed I Do".
Now when did you, you eventually organised a little band of your own didn't you?

Oh yes, yes. I had a band when, oh way before that. I had a band when I was about eight years old which was me playing piano, and I had a drummer and two little guys played tissue with a comb. And we used to, we used to play for parties. Give us two or three dollars a piece. Because I could play pretty, pretty nice piano at that time.
Well I mean a dollar was worth something then.
Sure it was, yes. We were only about thirteen, fourteen, fifteen, sixteen years old and as long as you had a drum and a piano the rest of the guys could hum. (LAUGHTER).
And I take it too that by this time you were getting records.
Oh yes. Learning, records were finally coming through of, some of a lot of Bessie Smith, mostly blues because in my home nearly everybody was blues crazy. Really liked
*Louis Armstrong's "Ding Dong Daddy" and "Confessin", both recorded in 1930, inspired Clayton more than others.
the blues and Bessie Smith was a big thing then. A big name. J.P. Johnson.
And of course, these people didn't come out to Parsons did they?
Never.
How far from Kansas City were you?
It's about 150 miles.
Oh, so I mean that would be a big trip to come, I mean....
Well, there used to be minstrel shows, like Billy King Minstrel Show which had my father's cousin Garbage Rogers from Chicago, he was.....
How, what was that first name?

Garbage Rogers. Marshall was his first name but his comedian name was Garbage Rogers. (LAUGHTER). I don't know........(LAUGHTER). He was a big, big shot in Chicago at the Regal Theater but he joined the Billy King Show. And I remember one time they came into Parsons, I must have been about eight years old and he needed my father's smoking jacket for a thing that he had in
his act. So I remember my dad letting him have it. You know, he was going to preach or, you know, one of those kind of things. Prince Albert, those Prince Albert coats.
And then there was the Drake and Walker Show, that came through there. With all beautiful girls and jazz musicians.
Well these were sort of touring vaudeville shows more or less, were they?
Yes.
When you say minstrel shows...
Yes, well they were black.
Did they have Mr. Bones?
Oh yes, yes.
Oh they did. This would be in the twenties?
Yes. Anywhere from '24 to '30.
Yes, I see.
Along those days. I had a friend whose mother ran away with one of those shows. He was a kid like I was, but his mother was very pretty and she ran away with the Drake and Walker Show
and never came back to Parsons.
Well I suppose in those sort of small country town like that the show had tremendous sort of glamor.

It did, it sure did. And of course, we used to get all of the circuses and they always had a side show. I always wanted to play in a circus, but I never did. They used to have the side shows, you know, when trumpet players would come out and play a hundred choruses of 'Sweet Sue' without taking down. And the pretty girls were dancing and comedians.....
I always liked that, but I never, never got the chance to play it because I was going to school.
Well that was one thing that I remember Edgar Battle and Eddie Burham they were with a circus.(at one time weren't they?)?
Yes and Roy Eldridge I believe was.......
I'm not (issuing them out?) purely of playing for the circus show, it's the shows outside.
No, I don't mean playing for the circus.
It's like a, it's like a travelling thing.
Jazzy Show, yes. A lot of jazz, a lot of chorus girls.
Yes, yes, that must have been, now what, what were the first name bands that you got to hear?
What do you mean?
Well I mean, you know, apart from the bands, I take it the bands with the circus were, you know, just groups of musicians.
Yes, yes there was no band.
I mean which were the first bands of any name......
Oh, that I got to listen to?
Yes, yes. That you heard.....
Oh, the first band that impressed me was George Lee, George E. Lee out of Kansas City, Missouri.
And what was it you liked about them?

Oh I liked everything about them. But I liked, I liked, they were sharp, they wore nice clothes and they had nice instruments. They could play nicely together and George himself and Julid Lee .........
Julia was the piano player?
That was his sister. They had a really beautiful band and Julia and George could both sing. That was before they had mikes. They used to sing with those plastic megaphones.

And George was, all of them were just nice looking and they all had big automobiles, Cords. You remember the old Cord automobiles. They had long, beautiful cars. And they had a trumpet player that I liked very much and I was impressed that they made in those days, they were making fifteen dollars a night which was a lot of money I thought.
Well it is in a sense.
At that time and still he La wasn't top notch band. Benny Moten was the top band.
But I mean fifteen dollars a night then....
And then, it was like...

Right, right. Sure. And they had a trumpet player named Bob Russel that I was crazy about because he had, when he opened his case, when he opened his case there was a slide trumpet, a mellophone a French Horn, a Catch trumpet which is about four feet long and a conventional trumpet. And he played all of these and he talked to me. I just decided then that I wanted to play trumpet, not piano.

So I got my dad to get me a little cornet. I had a little cornet and I practiced on it. That was my first horn until Christmas came and they got me a Buescher. My mother brought me a Buescher. So we played it.
A Buescher was almost a big instrument in those days.

It was one of them, yes. I wouldn't play much more on the piano. I just kind of switched. I didn't play piano any more until I got to Kansas City. Just before I joined Basie, there was no trumpet jobs open so I played piano in a little honky tonk place called The Florida Blossom.
Well how well could you play?
I could play very good.
Really?
Yes. Sometimes I'm sorry now I didn't keep it up, but I was a very, very good pianist.
But this of course, was to be useful to you.
Oh yes, in arranging, yes. You know the keyboard, and it's very easy to arrange if you are a good pianist/guitar player, if you know chords.
Well, in those days, oh of course you'd heard Louis Armstrong's records by this time?

Yes, But I, oh yes, I mustn't forget this. There was a fellow who came back to Parsons from Kansas City, his name was Raymond Jones, and he had played at the Eblon Theater in Kansas City in which Basie....
That's EBLON?

Yes. Eblon where you see, it was a show house. It was like all of the carnivals, two or three carnivals in one show and they'd have a movie. Then they'd have this big show. And he played in the pit, violin. So he came back from Kansas

City and organised, his nickname was Mouse because was a little cat he like Mousey Alexander the drummer here, you know, so his name was Mouse Jones, but his real name was Raymond. So he organised a jazz group called, 'Mouse and his Music'. (LAUGHTER).
That was my very, very first band that I played in and I played first trumpet and a little kid named Clarence Trice played second trumpet.
Clarence Trice?
Clarence Trice, yes. He used to play with Andy Kirk, later on he got to be with Andy Kirk.
TRICE?

TRICE. And Mouse and his Music, we played different little small towns around Parsons. But that's where I first heard Louis Armstrong, the first record I ever heard was of Louis Armstrong. And I was quite impressed, you know with Louis. Everybody was quite impressed.

I remember one of my acts with Mouse, I had to put on a top hat a long silk coat and take a plunger, and I had some kind of a preaching act I had to do (at)a plunger, to "St. James' Infirmary." That was my act.
Yes well 'St. James' Infirmary' was one of George E. Lee's numbers. I remember when he recorded that.
Yes, that's right.
Well Mouse and his Music, this was professional but around Parsons was it?
Yes, we got paid for our little jobs. We didn't get paid too much. Five or ten dollars.
How old were you now though?
I was about seventeen I guess.
Oh, I see. Now what did you do about school all this time?
I was going to school.
Yes. How far did you go then?
I went, I played around Parsons until 1929. In 1929 I left home. Me and a friend of mine caught a freight train and rode all the way out to Los Angeles.
Why did you do that?
Well we just was, Parsons was kind of boring. There wasn't anything to do. And I had had a friend of mine that had moved to California
and he used to write back and tell me how beautiful, which it was beautiful.
Well what was his name?
Theodore Booker.
Theodore Booker?
Yes. But he wasn't a musician.
Oh I see.
He was not, just one of my best friends. And so another friend of mine Jack Medlock.
Medlock?
Yes. We decided we were going to go to California as soon as school was out.
Was he a musician?
No. He got a saxophone the same time I got my trumpet. He played one concert in church, not a concert, one song in church and never picked it up again. He didn't like it.

Anyway we ran off to California and I still had a year to go in highschool. But anyway I ran off to California. I wasn't playing good enough then to join a band, far from it. So I worked out in California working in different jobs. I worked in a pool hall, which was a tough job because it was in a tough district.
What did you do there then?

I had to rack the balls, stop fights and feed the dogs. Everything. Saturday nights used to be awful. It was on Twelfth Street in Los Angeles, Twelfth Street and Central which at that time was a bad ......

I used to walk around with a little hatchet. Sometimes we had to break up fights with hatchets. And I stayed there until, the whole summer. Then I went back home. I saved enough money to buy a bus fare back home. I finished highschool.
You didn't do any playing out there?

Not then, no. I went back to school and I finished my highschool. Then when that was over I went to work for a cousin of mine in Atchison, Kansas who had a rock quarry there. I went up there and worked because I said I was never going to ride a freight train again as long as I lived. Because they were so dirty and disgusting, you know.
Now when you said ride a freight train, where did you ride on it?
All over it. And all in it. We got in all kinds of cars.
What about that thing the hobos used to do, riding the rods underneath. Did you do any of that?
We did that. We rode beneath, we rode inside, we rode on top.
Well isn't that dangerous?
Yes.
I mean if you fell off to sleep you'd have had it?

Yes. Sure. And we used to ride, we'd be on top of a car, sometimes we had to run. We didn't want to, we'd just catch the first car we could, maybe we'd get a box car. And if we wanted to get to a low car we might have to run fifteen box cars before we'd come to a low one. And we used to run on top of these things in the dead of night. Three o'clock in the morning sometimes.
How flat are the tops of those things?
Well, the center is flat but the sides are sloped, you know.
Well how wide is that Flat surface?
About eighteen inches, a foot and a half.
So you're reasonably safe as long as the thing doesn't ......
Yes, as long as the smoke you the smoke is lying flat, it comes right in your face. But you've got to stay on there. It's dangerous. Very dangerous, especially at night. It's very dangerous.
But you'd walk, you wouldn't go on all fours?

No, we'd walk or run if we could. One time we got locked in a celery car and couldn't get out. And they side-tracked that car and wasn't going to use it for three months. And we were in there pounding, trying to get out. There was no celery in there so they weren't going to use the car.
Oh, I see.
And we just pounded me and the other guy and we got scared and started crying. And we didn't know it had been side-tracked. And finally one little Mexican guy heard us pounding and went up
and broke the lock and let us out. Because we would have starved easily in there if we hadn't got out of there.
Yes, that's a kind of horrible death. Well when you get back, after this trip back on the freight cars, you don't want to do it any more?

I don't, No, you see that freight trip alone was something I would never in my life forget. Because you see in those days there wasn't the civil rights movement. This is in '29, that's it. Now one time we went to Denver and we thought we were catching the train, okay, the next freight train. We get off and make a change. We thought we were going West and we were going South. We didn't know we were going South for all long time. And, you know, naturally there are other guys who ride these trains, they don't know where they are going. They don't care, they just ride, the real hobos.

And we found out that, when we did find out we were going South we were in Texas and we got off right away. Going to catch the next train back to Denver and then be sure we got a train going West to Los Angeles. So we got off the train and we were,

me and my friend were just laying under some trees waiting— out in the country not in the city, waiting for the next train coming back on on the same line, you know, in the next direction. And all of a sudden two car loads of Texas police came up to us and the first thing they did was, which you are the two people that raped that woman about twenty miles from here.

We said, we didn't, naturally you know, we just got in. They said, No, you're the ones that raped that woman. So they took us in a car, they took us back to some little town, I don't remember the name, of the town now, and they took us down in the bottom of the railroad station and it was about, oh I guess 7 o'clock. There must have been about seven of these guys. So they formed a circle and all of them got, they got clubs and every other thing and made us get in the middle of the circle and made us dance.
You know, they said, 'can you dance?' We said, yes, we can dance. And well, they made us dance and they accused us of everything.
Were they beating you?
No. No, they didn't hit us.
But if we hadn't danced maybe, you know. I learned to

buck dance from watching the minstrel shows. So about ten o'clock that night they took us out and put us in the street. And there were about four car loads of guys lined up behind us and they walked us way, way back out into the country. And as we were going me and my friend 'cause you know, in those days, there had been so many inching and things.
Well I, that was, yes.

So boy we said, Jesus Christ, what did we do to get into this kind of crap and all we could see behind was these four or five car loads and they were all full of guys, full of these people out of this little town in Texas.

And they marched us way, way out and then you know, I don't know what happened, but I believe that somebody in that bunch convinced them not to go through with what they were probably thinking about. Because one time, we were out there about seven miles in the country, which they wouldn't have followed us that far for no reason.
And you were walking and they were driving?
We were walking. They were driving slow, yes. All we could see were headlights.
We would look around and they were still there you know.
Maybe there were hoping you'd run?
We didn't run.
Yes because then they would probably have shot you.

Maybe. Oh yes, if we had tried to get away but we didn't do that. So finally they all of them turned around and went back. And went all the way back to the city. And after we waited about an hour to be sure they were gone, then we sneaked back to the railroad tracks and caught a train and went on back to Denver.
Then we went West, then we got out there with no trouble. But I'll never forget late at night on the highway in Texas with four or five carloads of guys following you.
Yes, you must have been scared.
Yes, I was. Wxixyxaxxax
Well you didn't know what was going to happen.
I know, we didn't know. There was no way we could know. But we, of course being young
No, but that wasn't.....
I think somebody just convinced them that they......
I mean in the South it was really just an excuse to......
Sure, sure. Certainly in those days.
And I mean, Texas was just as bad as the South in those days.*
Yes.
That was also added to your unwillingness to travel on a freight train.

Yes, that and the fact that it took me about ten days to get that dirt and grime out of my face. You know, it was, it took us six days to get there. And you just get so dirty you can't get it out, it kind of wear out. Especially you know like I said, running on top of the train and all that smoke and cinders get into your face. I said, never again. Never again for me.
So we finally ended up in Los Angeles and we had a friend from Parsons there who was a
*Incidents like this have happened in Parsons, Kansas, but usually provoked by people from other southern states. Some cowboys from Texas tried it a few times.---Clayton's note.

prize fighter. A good one, a welterweight. His name was Charlie Long. Charlie got us a hotel room and we got cleaned up. Then he found us some jobs. He found the job for me in the pool hall. My buddy had a job in a gasoline station oiling cars. So we did that until it was time for me to go back to finish, because I decided I wanted to finish highschool.
Well what was California like then? I mean that must have been sort of just.....
It was beautiful.
It was sort of booming then wasn't it?
Yes. There wasn't any smog out there then. The air was fresh and it was just a beautiful place. Beautiful, a real beautiful place.
But the work opportunities were not that good then. I mean there was no question of playing trumpet on this first trip?
Oh well I didn't, I wasn't good enough.
Oh yes I see, yes.
I wasn't good enough. I had the trumpet, but I wasn't good enough. Still about a
year and a half later after I went back home and finished school and then went back out there.
How did you go back this time?
On the bus.
On the bus.
Yes, I worked on my cousins' rock quarry to save up enough money and I took the Greyhound bus.
How many days would that take?
Greyhound bus? Three or four if I'm not mistaken.
Could you sleep in the bus?
Yes.
Well who was out in California playing when you arrived now?
At this time?
Yes, when you. came back.

Well I don't know you see because I didn't, I didn't know the musicians. I remember one theater, the Lincoln Theater in Los Angeles was where we would go every Sunday night and they would have a show. And I can only remember one fellow there and his name was Alton Reid, a drummer. He had the band in the theater.
But there was a club there called, the Club Alabam. It was run by Curtis Mosby. They had a beautiful band in there too.
What was his partner, Reb Spikes or something? Some such name? Didn't Curtis Mosby have a partner?
I don't remember now.
Oh well....... Was ( ?) in the pit?

No, it was just a nightclub. It was a night club with a lot of chorus girls. But see, at that age I didn't, I didn't know anybody. I remember James Porter was a trumpet player. You know I often wonder whether James Porter was the guy who Jelly Roll Morton wrote 'King Porter' for. *
Really?
I don't know. I've often wondered that because.....
Was he a good trumpet player?
Yes. A fat little guy. He looked like Louis a little.
Oh yes? Where did he come from do you know?
*see note, p. 38.
No I don't. I don't know where he was from. But he was pretty famous out there as a trumpet player.
Yes. I mean, did he have his own band?
No, he worked in Curtis Moseby's band.
Oh yes, yes.

And I know Jelly Roll was out in California and I just wondered where he got the inspiration for "King Porter Stamp". I've often wondered but now Porter is dead so I don't know if I'll ever find that out.
This Jake Porter that is still out there, he was no relation of James Porter?
I don't think so, no. I don't think so. I don't think he was.
Well on this return trip, what did you do when we went back this time?
When I went back to California? After finishing school?
Yes. Now you've had a year and a half more training on the horn?
Yes, that's right.
Well who taught you? Or was it a matter of......

Just being at home. Still playing with the church band while I'm doing this year in school. Still playing with them. Then there were some more little bands around Kansas that whenever they had jobs they would always call me to work with them.
It maybe a town twenty five miles from my home, but if I wasn't doing anything they'd call me. Just like they do when New York would call you to work in Newark, somewhere like that.
What sort of way were you playing in those days? I mean were you playing, were you improvising then?

Oh yes. I was improvising but mostly my own improvisations because I didn't know too much about, I didn't have too many records of, in those days Red Nichols was pretty good. He was about one of the best jazz trumpet player, but I never tried to play like him.
And I just played jazz the way I felt like I wanted to play it. And I really didn't start to play like anybody until after school when I went back
to California. I used to learn solos from Louis Armstrong and Cootie. Those were the main two.
Where did you hear Cootie? Now this was, oh this would be with Duke?
With Duke. And I remember one of my friends in California was a tenor player Pete Kinard.

I think that Russell's band..
Well you see he made some inbetween California now.
Yes he did. Well I can easily check that. I mean, you'd know. Then of course Louis always did say that he liked Guy Lombardo's band.
Yes. Yes he did. He always said it and I think he meant it. He played with him didn't he out in Long Island?
Yes. But I think it's, I think you can see what it was he liked. You know, the sort of, well 'Sweethearts on Parade' was another one of his big things. That was a Guy Lombardo thing wasn't it?
Yes, right.
Well now, where do we go from here? We've finished with California, this ......
Well I just didn't know. I didn't want to go too fast.
No, I don't want you to.
Where were we? About Louis.
Did you, did you know by this time, I mean did you know Lionel Hampton and did you know Lawrence Brown?
Oh yes. I'd known Lionel. You see, with my band later we went into the Cotton Club too. But....
When was this before or after you went to China?
This was before.
Before?
Yes.
Oh well, we must go into that then.

Yes. And Lionel, you see, I had a boy named Kid Lips Hacket that I used to play with. Before we went to the Cotton Club I also played with a show, an all black show, called Irving C. Miller and his Brown Skin Models. And my whole band, we played for that show. And there's where we picked up a bass player named Red Cullendar. You know he's out in California now.
Sure.
Red was with the show before we joined it, so he joined our band. But I had a

drummer named Kid Lips who was in the show too. A wonderful drummer. So we played quite a few dates for Irving C. Miller and it was a good show. Then we came back to Los Angeles and left the show to go into Frank Sebastian's Cotton Club. Because Frank wanted me to come in there. But I had to let my drummer off and keep Lionel because Lionel stayed in there no matter who came in. House (band ?) (man ?).
Well he was hired by the ....
He stayed there because he did his acts all over his thing, he did his little part of the show.
Was he using the vibraphone in his show then?
Yes.
Oh, he was?
But not very much because he was mainly the drummer.
Yes.

I don't care who came in there, they had to take Lionel. So I couldn't use my drummer. I just paid him and he could do whatever he wanted to, but we paid him and Lionel was getting his own pay from Frank Sebastian as a specialty artist.
Would he go into a big drum solo?
Yes. Yes, he did that. Beating on everybody's head, beating on the floor and ended up back on the drums, you know, throwing the sticks. So we played Frank Sebastian's Cotton Club for a long time.
Then we came out and I, let's see what did I do then? It's about that time that .....
What sort of place was Frank Sebastian's Cotton Club?

Oh, it was a beautiful place. It was in Culver City. A big green and white beautiful building and all, what made it so nice, was that nearly everybody that came in there were movie people. Money was just every where.
It wasn't open air. It was..... no.
No, no.
I don't know why I thought it might have been.
No, it was inside. Very plush. And Frank was a very good host. He was a nice, tall, nice.
Was it something like the Cotton Club in New York do you think?
No, no. It was quite different.

Quite different. There were no other buildings around it. You know, like the Cotton Club here. It was just a big beautiful building, with beautiful lights. You could see it a half mile away. A mile away with all these beautiful lights. Frank Sebastian's Cotton Club.
How big was it?
It was a big building.
Oh, it was?
Yes.
It would hold a lot of people?

A lot of people. Every night was like New Year's Eve. Every night was something different. With all these movie people coming in there you see. Nothing but movie people. And he had the best acts. All the acts he had/you know. Cab Calloway, and his band was there. He had the Mills Brothers. Louis, Fats Waller. You know, it was we had a real big time band.
Well what, how did Fats Waller perform?
He did good, very well.
But I mean would he come with a group or would he.......

No, he came with, by himself. He played with Les Hite. So we stayed with Frank and then we came out and we made tours up and down, we always were making tours from Los Angeles to Vancouver whenever we weren't doing anything.
This is the Pantages circuits again?

Yes, yes. While we were going up and down travelling from Los Angeles you know, to Canada and back, at the same time I had met a girl that worked as a dancer in the Cotton Club and she was there when everybody was there. In other words, they stayed there year in and out. She had worked there for years, two or three years I guess.
So she knew Louis and she knew Fats Waller and she knew Cab, she knew everybody. And I met her and he name was Gladys, Gladys Henderson.
Henderson?
Henderson, yes. They called her Derby. Because she used to dance like a fellow here named Derby Wilson. I don't know if you know him or not?
No, but I know the name.
All the people that came from

the East said, you dance just like Derby Wilson. So she got them that name Derby Henderson. They called her Derby. And Derby and I, we kind of liked each other quite a bit and we went together for a long time.
Weatherford
Then there was a fellow named Teddy who came from....
Chicago.

He was originally a big pianist before Earl Hines. He had been to the Orient and had come back especially to pick up a black band like Duke Ellington's, 'cause Duke was just a big hit all over the world, you know. So he was originally supposed to visit Los Angeles, Chicago and then New York. Select a band and try to get this band to go back to Shang Hai.

So he heard our band, my band, and he heard Les Hite's band and right away he liked my band. And he didn't go to Chicago. He didn't go to New York, he just stopped right there and signed us up to ask me if we would go. And I said, yes, you know, if we, this was about '33 or '34 which wasn't too far behind the Depression. The salaries were still low.
So, he offered me six months and the guys were

to get a hundred dollars a week, which at that time was quite a bit of money. So I paid the guys a hundred dollars a week. But before we went, before we had even planned to go, there was a question of whether my girl friend Derby, could go without being married. We had to be married, you know, to go.

So we really didn't know whether we wanted to get married or not. We knew we liked each other but we didn't know that was well enough to get married on. So we decided well we will be leaving pretty soon. The best thing we can do is to go down and apply for a licence, get it all set. If we don't marry, okay. And if we do decide to marry, we've got the licence and we won't have to go through that.

So we went down city hall and got a licence. And it came out in the paper the next day which we didn't know. In the 'intentions to wed' department. My name and her name. Now at this time, Duke Ellington is in California making a movie called 'Check and Double Check'. No, no, 'Murder at the Vanities'. That's what it was. Yes, 'Murder at the Vanities'. And my wife was working in the picture. So Duke knew my wife and he knew me. He knew I was, there were only two big bands in Los Angeles, Les Hite and myself.

So, he looks in the paper and he says, oh, he says, Buck and Derby think they are going to sneak down and get married and not going to tell anybody about it. So all of the chorus girls read it and so Duke says, let's give them a big send off.

So all the chorus girls, we weren't supposed to know anything about this. They got together. They arranged with the Head of the Paramount Studios to cut off a day from twelve o'clock, to cut off all the actors. They built a special bandstand for the band. Sonny Greer was way up high. They had newsreels at the wedding. They employed the Mills Brothers to sing. Ivy Anderson sang, was hired to sing and they had a cake so big, they had a great big huge cake.

And Mae West was there. All of the actors were there. George Raft was there. But the night before that Freddie Jenkins and George Raft and I were, we were shooting craps in a after hours place on Central Avenue and you know, like they were saying, well you better enjoy tonight because you'll be married, you'll be an old married man soon.
And I wasn't supposed to know. But see they kept saying you are going to be an old married man
pretty soon. So I found out from Freddie Jenkins …….
You thought
They were just ribbing you.

Yes. He said, are you going to be there? I says where? He says you better be there. This was about five o'clock in the morning and I was supposed to get married about one o'clock, after we had left the after hours place.
So I went home and finally the next morning somebody called me and told me to be at the studio at one o'clock. But I knew then what it was.
Who had tipped you off? Or had you sort of guessed?

I had guessed already because Freddie had almost told me and said, you better be there, and you know the other guys, old man. well you've gonna be in One o'clock I'm supposed to be there. So I started thinking, do I want to, do I want to? Do I want to go through with that? I didn't know that so much had been prepared. And from Los Angeles to Hollywood, Paramount Studios, at that time was about a 45 minute ride, at least. Because they didn't have the thruway you see.
Well how would you go out there?

You would go out in a car but it was a long...... long ride. It's like going to Queens XxXxXxXxXx only worse. It takes longer. So I just don't know what to do. I'm thinking. I didn't have any money I was broke. And I didn't know whether I wanted to get married. China or no China, I didn't know whether..... So I was, I was leaning up against a telephone pole and I could see everybody was going out to Hollywood. All of the actors, all the singers, Nat King Cole was one. And I was leaning up against the telephone pole. And they were saying are you going to make it? Are you going to make it?

I says, I don't know. They said, we're going on out anyway, you know. So I stood right by that telephone pole you see, trying to make up my mind. I stayed there, twelve o'clock. I still was there at one o'clock. That was when I should have been in Hollywood. And I was there until about one, almost one thirty when the guys in my band, Teddy Buckner and some others....
Oh he was in your band?
Yes. He was in the band after Earl Dancer.
Oh, I see, yes.

So they pulled me in the car. They said, well if you can't make up your mind we'll make it up for you. And they pulled me in the car and I got out there about almost an hour and a half late. And boy, Duke had his hands, his head in his hands like this. see Duke You never worry much do you? Boy he was very upset. Jesus Christ what have I done? If this guy don't show up I'm in deep trouble. So I, when I showed up my wife's mother was going crazy. She was crying and raising hell and everybody was all upset because I should have been there at one and I got there at two, way after two.

But when I got there everybody came to life. Cootie growled the wedding march. And the pastor married us with the news cameras right down on us. All the chorus girls and everybody was sitting around like a big coliseum and the Mills Brother sang and Ivy Anderson sang. And they had the wedding. I was married. And that's the way I got married.
And you really hadn't decided about it right up to the end?
Yes, and I think I was right. Because we didn't stay married very long. No after we
got to China we didn't stay married. We had to stay married, we had to stay together [any way] over there. But when we came back we just didn't make it, too much fanfare.
And if it hadn't been for that, maybe we would never of got married.
Right. Of course the China thing was pushing you into it really.
Yes, that's right. Because we had to be married. I couldn't take her over as a girl friend.
Well what, I mean you don't have to talk about it, but was it that she was sort of too much involved with the sort of theatrical thing to, or did she not want to settle down? Or what?
Well I don't really....
Or was it temperament?
Not really, no. [I don't really know.] She was just temperamental. It was just one of those things.
Maybe you didn't either. Maybe you you were too young to be married.
Well that's what I think. I really do. I think so. You see she and I were both the same age. We were both born on the same day, the
same year, exactly the same.
The same day and year?
Yes. My wife I'm married to now was born on the same day. The same month but not the same year.
How strange. How extraordinary. Well that was a most unusual coincidence. You present wife is the same day?
That's right. November 12th. My first wife was November 12th.
Isn't that strange?
Yes. Mine is November 12th.
Well anybody might think you picked them out for that, but I don't imagine that was....

No, I actually didn't believe my second wife. When I was divorced from my first wife I didn't meet my second wife until I was in the army. Somehow I asked her when her birthday was and she said, November 12th. And I didn't believe it. She took me home and showed me the Bible. Her birthday in the Bible was November 12th.
That's the most amazing thing I've ever heard of. I mean it's very unusual to...
Yes, yes it is even to find one.
But I've been married twice and.....
And also when you're in professional life like that, I mean it's hard isn't it? Because you're travelling and....

Yes, you're not really sure of what you really want to do. And that was why we went down to have the license in case we did want to do it we didn't have to. If we wanted to do it at the last minute, we had the license. But they picked it up from there and we didn't get a chance to do what we had planned. We had to go through with that, after all those preparations.
Duke Ellington's big secret just ( ?).
He meant to. I mean I know he (meant well ?). He came down to the boat when we went to China. Took pictures of us all on the boat. I've got these pictures.
You've still got them?
Yes, Duke was only thirty. '33 or '34.
If, if they should decide to do any ing of publish this interview, that's what, they should use those pictures.
Yes.
Do you have pictures of the actual wedding?

Yes. But now I'll tell you they are in a book. Sure I've got pictures. I've got pictures of the wedding and pictures of Duke on the boat. I never did get the newsreels. Duke got the newsreels. My mother saw it in Kansas. After we'd gone then it came out on the news. But I never saw it because we were out on the sea. It took us three weeks to get to China.
I wonder if Duke has still got it?
He may have.
He wouldn't know where it is I bet. (LAUGHTER). That was quite something then wasn't it?
Yes it was. That was the biggest, for a long time, I don't know if the records ever been broken, but that was the biggest thing that they had had at Paramount, at Paramount studios.
Well, I've seen pictures of the set from 'Murder at the Vanities' and that is a sort of great big built up, like a half circle with the chorus girls and the band all spread out in the circle.
That was probably what they used wasn't it?
I don't know whether that was it or whether they built it. They had carpenters that could set that up and then it could have been.
Well they used pictures of that set in the publicity for the picture. But it was certainly very effective.
CLAYTON: Well, it could have been.
Yes, see all the girls, everything was up and girls all around and people sitting up and throwing rice down on us.
That's right. So that sent you off to China?
Yes, that's when we went to China.
And how long were you there?
In China?
Yes.
We were in China two years.
You were there two years?
Yes, '34 to '36. I came back in '36.
And Teddy Buckner went?
Teddy Buckner went, Bumps Coughy Myers went, ?) Roberts went. He came to New York with Basie on the first ......
How do you pronounce that?
Couchy.
And that's spelled?
It's an indian name. CAUGHEY. An indian name. Yes, he went. Now there's not many others.
Was Teddy Weatherford with the band?
No.
Oh, he'd just come down to the (?).
Oh he came back with us.
Oh he did?

Yes. And he would play with us but when we played a specialty like 'Rhapsody in Blue', you see Teddy was working three or four clubs in one night. He'd play 45 minutes here. Leave here and go across town, 45 minutes there. Leave there and go another place. And he was playing four clubs twice a night.
Well how do you rate him as a piano player as compared with somebody like Fats Waller or (Earl?).
Well he was, he was the greatest
(forger?). Yes, Earl used to try to play like Teddy, when Earl was young.
Well the thing is you know, you don't hear much (recording?).
No you don't.
And if Teddy makes those records in Paris around 1937...
He was late.
Well, I know, but he wasn't always.
I know, that was '37.
In '37 he was not much more than....
Yes, but his best days were in the early twenties. When Louis first came in from Chicago they were both in the Vendome theater.
But do you think then that he sort of deteriorated or....
Well, I don't know. You see he still played beautiful when we went over. But I mean, actually, he, his best thing to me was playing 'Rhapsody in Blue' which was a different ....
Sort of a show music?
Right, right.
Well that, you see that's the point because those things he made in Paris, they are kind
of simple but I mean they are good. I mean you wouldn't compare him as a pianist with Earl or Fats?
No, but well what I would have liked to have heard him when he was in the Vendamo theater. Then I could say, but as you say, they weren't, he didn't record much in those days.
No, there's one, there's one thing he plays on with a band with Louis Armstrong with Erskine Tate's band for d he comes in chorus. A little like Fats Waller.
Is it he?
(Isn't going to knock you out, or anything
I don't think, I don't think that he ever played up to what Earl Hines did later. You know when Earl was the ......
Now you know Lois Deppe the singer don't you?
Yes.

Well his wife was a piano player and she was in Chicago and she said that when Earl came to Chicago they played together, you know they used to run around together and played together. But she said that in her opinion Teddy Wetherford was never their equal.
Yes, I'd say that too. But see Earl got better.
Yes, that's right, he went ahead.
When Earl first met Teddy, Teddy was better, But when Earl did stretch out there was nobody that could touch Earl. You know what I mean?
Right.
Father Hines was really the ......
Yes. I mean it was still a different thing to what Fats and James were playing.
Yes, yes. It's just like to me Louis Armstrong admiring King Oliver. Later on he did some, much greater things than King Oliver did.

Yes. Well I mean Louis went ahead of King Oliver in terms of virtuosity and imagination. But you would not really say, I wouldn't really say that Earl went ahead of Fats and James in terms of virtuosity?
Well no... in style...
In imagination, yes. And then of course you would go along with him until Tatum comes in.
Mmm.
Well now what, when you get to
Shanghai what impression did that make on you?
On that was a beautiful, best I believe probably the best two years of my life.
Really?

Yes. China was great. I don't know, now I wonder if it was just because I was young. But it was so, so different. The whole country, the customs. The dress and we were treated so nicely. And we had such a, such a good time. Everybody was so nice there.
Where did you stay? I mean where did you play first of all?
We played in this big casino called the Canidrome ballroom.
CANIDROME?
Yes. And they had dog races every night in the Canidrome.
What do you mean?
Greyhounds, yes.
Well that was illegal to have dog racing wasn't it?
No, no they had it over there.
Well when did they first start to go for greyhound racing in Europe?
I don't know.
It seems to me that that, no...
But they had it in China.
They did?

Yes. When we got off the band-there were still, there were four ballrooms in this place and we used to go out and watch them. Watch the greyhounds race between sets. And they had, it was in the French Quarter.
Oh that was when they had like for....
European settlements. French settlement they called it, but all of the Americans and English, there were all of us living there. But they called it...
But there was a sort of an international..... Yes I see. Each country had a ....

They all lived there, yes. International settlement. French, the Americans, the Russians, the English. And we had a beautiful Master of Ceremonies and Mistress of Ceremonies. I don't remember his name. Her name was Ursula Preston.
You better spell that.
Ursula Preston.
Oh Ursula? Preston?

Yes. Both of them were from England. And they were ballroom dancers. And they announced our band every night and they were so immaculate and we were dressed in all, we bought so many different uniforms. We had eight or ten different uniforms.
We had white tails, black tails and grey tails. White suits. (LAUGHTER).
It's amazing.

Yes, you see those tailors made everything by hand and so cheap. You couldn't believe. You got a suit for such a cheap amouht. So we really got stocked up on clothes. Because it would cost us too much money to buy in the States. All of them tailor made to everybody. And all these acts would come over from America and we would play for their acts. And it was just a wonderful two years.
Not the whole two years because we had some trouble there.
Well of course you would play to dance?
Right.
But did you tell me once that you played some concerts on Sunday?
We did. It was what we call Tea dances on Sunday afternoons. Like from three to five.
And then what would you do at those?

Well we would play concert, We played not only jazz, we called it light opera. Yes we played light opera like Ravel's 'Bolero'. 'Rhapsody in Blue'. We had quite a few things. We could play a couple of hours of that.
Is this where Teddy would come in?
No, he didn't play at the tea dances. When he didn't play 'Rhapsody in Blue' we had Eddie Beal.
Oh was he with you?
Yes. You know Eddie
Yes. I've heard....
Charley Beal's brother.
Yes, yes.
Eddie Beal was on the piano. He was our original piano. Teddy was, you know.
I see. Well of course the one thing,
I take it that this time you were playing dance music you weren't playing nothing but jazz. I mean you were playing waltzes?
Oh yes.
Tangos and everything weren't you?
Oh yes. Waltzes.....
Well what kind of response did you get to sort of out and out jazz performances?
We got, very, very, very good.
You did?

Yes. We had good arrangements. We had very good arrangements and there were a lot of American musicians over in China at that time too. And they would all come down and listen to us. There were a lot of marines over there and we were always invited to play on their bases. Play for the marines.
That was where your one bit of trouble came from though? Wasn't it?
Yes. But not from the marines. Just from one, one bad marine out of the whole bunch. You know what I mean.
What happened?
Well this guy, he was an ex-marine. He didn't belong to the marines when we were there. He was kicked out of the marines. He had stolen some

money in the States and he had ran off to Shang-hai. He had robbed a bank I believe it was. Now I don't know when he was in the marines. Whether it was before he did this or after. But anyway, he was a marine and he used to box, a pugilist in the marine corps.

So one night we were playing. At this particular time there were some girls from California that had been brought over to star in the show. About six of them. All blondes. And they were called the Hollywood Blondes. And we had rehearsed their act and played it /and we knew it. And one night this Miss Ursula Preston from London announced that now we are going to have such and such and these girls have just come from the States and they are the famous Hollywood Blondes. And I was supposed to turn around and give the down beat so they would go right into the music.

So I noticed this fellow walk in. I didn't know who he was. But he was with two Russian girls and the girls had been in there the night before, you see. I don't know what their names was. But one of them had jerked a handkerchief out of my pocket that had B.C. on it. And I knew her because we had had all these pretty handkerchiefs made with a trumpet sewn in it and B.C. and everybody, they all had them, the whole band.

But she had jerked mine out and I never see it any more. The next night she came in with this guy and another girl I'd never seen before. And while the Mistress of Ceremonies is announcing the Hollywood Blondes the two girls come in and they sit down. He don't sit down, he's standing up there and looking at me. And I just looked back, you know, I just could see something was wrong. (LAUGHTER).

I looked back and he still didn't sit down. So I turned around and gave the down beat. And here comes all the blondes running on the floor. So I, I said to myself, I'm going to, you know, I'm going to ask this fellow what's wrong. So I figured out while they were dancing I'm going to go around this side and, you know, ask him what was wrong you know, or something like that. You know, why would he, no, you see, before that when I was looking at him he says, turn your eyes the other way, you black bastard.
Oh I see.

You see. So the girls all kicking up their feet and I went over, I never did get to his table because the guy hit me and I didn't even see the punch coming. You know, I say, he had been a fighter before.

So he hit me right between the eyes. Right between the eyes. I had two black eyes for a long time. But I remember, the next thing I remember I'm down on one knee shaking my head like that. Those girls were still kicking all over me. And the band had jumped off the stand and they got this guy and they're beating the hell out of him.

And he was hollering, help. I tell you who was there that night was Madame Chiang Kai Chek and her sister. One of them she went later with the communists and Madame Chiang Kai Chek is still with the General. They were there that night. And so this guy's hollering, help, help, why don't some of you white son of a bitches help me, help me.

Nobody would help him because they saw everything. So my guitar player broke his guitar over his head and Teddy Buckner was kicking him and the whole band just jumped, when he hit me they jumped right off the stand and grabbed him. Then when they saw I could stand up, they let me get on him. And he and I battled all out into the bathroom, And I was just sitting on his chest, you know, I was trying to kill him.
So finally, a reporter, an American reporter

there said, okay Buck, okay, you know, just like that to get me up which was better than trying to pull me off of him. So I got off the guy and his head was all swollen and he went out and came back. And we all thought he had a gun when he came back because he was all bloodied up. But he didn't have a gun. He had lost his wallet and was trying to find the wallet. (LAUGHTER).

The next day he sued the Canidrome. He sued all of them for non-protection. But when all of the witnesses that were there came up and told exactly what happened he lost the case. He had to pay court charges. He had to pay everything. You know, because he was so wrong.

But I, for about three weeks, I couldn't go anywhere without a body guard because this guy was from Atlanta, Georgia and all those Southerners over there had theatened that if I came to work the next day they were going to blow, they were going to have a machine gun out there or blow up the Canidrome, if I came to work.
Well who theatened this?
These White Southern people that were living in China. You see at that time if they knew

somebody from Georgia got beat up, they didn't know. They knew that I was a band leader. So my life was threatened. And for about three weeks I couldn't go anywhere unless I had two or three people right on me, my body guards.
I still had two pretty black eyes. So finally the Canidrome....
Do you think that the handkerchief had something to do with it?
I never did find out.
You never found out?

No. I never saw the girl any more. But I knew she had jerked my, now whether he had seen the handerchief and knew with the trumpet on it and my name was Buck Clayton. That could have been that, I don't know.
But at the same time if it were that, you wouldn't have thought he would have come to the place with her.
I just don't know. But I just wonder if that's what triggered it.
Yes, it sounds as though it might.
He called me that name so loud and everybody could hear. You know, I said, I know something has got to be wrong, with him.
So eventually they had to let us out because they were afraid they were going to get blown up.
Well you mean this, at the Canidrome?
Yes.
Oh, so it was really a very bad thing then?
Pretty bad. But see we opened very shortly in another club and this club says we proudly announce Buck Clayton. Because he didn't care if they were going to.....
What was the name of this other club?
You know I have to look in my book to find it out. But it was a French name. It had a French name. (SEE MR. CLAYTON'S NOTES) [Casa Nova Club]
How long were you there?
Oh we were there about six or eight months. We had done quite a bit at the Canidrome. We had done about eight or ten months.
I see. So you built up a big local following?
Yes, we did. You know who
was a youngster over there who used to come and see me was Langston Hughes.
Really?
He was a young man just learning to write.
What was he doing?
He was over there writing.
Oh he was? Didn't you tell me once that Madame Ch'iang Kai Chek was trying to learn to tap dance?
SEE MR. CLAYTON'S NOTES.*
[Yes,] she would come down every Saturday afternoon and Duke Upshaw who was one of the trombone players in the band was a good dancer.
Upshaw?
Yes, Duke Upshaw.
UPSHAW?

Yes. He was teaching her how to dance. Every Saturday she'd come down and spend a couple of hours learning how to dance. So you know, we were all pretty close together. And she and I'm so glad that she was there that night that this happened. So she testified and so on.

When I got back to New York less than ten days later, I had revived the interest in me and they sent me a greetings, "greetings". If I had never written they probably would have never called me. But I woke them up by asking for a new card then I get "greetings". (LAUGHTER).
That's really a funny way of referring to induction as greetings. (LAUGHTER).

"Greetings." So I went in. I was the first to go in Basie's band. But I didn't mind really. I did mind but what the heck, you just, all you can do is make the best of it, so I just decided to take it as a rest.

I didn't have to do one-nighters. I could sleep and eat good food. And eventually I got to like it. I kind of liked it because a lot of times all the soldiers would break their necks getting out of there on a Friday knowing they don't have to be back until Monday.
Well now, where were you?

I was in three camps. First I was in Camp Upton, New Jersey. Then I went to Camp Kilmer, no Camp Upton, Camp Shanks was second. That's in Orange, New Jersey. And it was there that I was out there with Sy Oliver and Mercer.
Ellington.
Yes, Bo' McCain was there and . A lot of people. And as I said, I began to pick up weight. I gained, I went from 160 pounds to 190 in the Army.
Well you were, you were sort of still a musician?
Oh yes.
Don't you have to do basic training or something first?

We, no. All I ever did was march, march, march, march. I could march, but they wouldn't let me shoot. They wouldn't let me shoot. They took me out one time to shoot the gun and I shot the gun and it popped me and hit me right in the mouth. So I couldn't play the trumpet for days.
How did that.......
The gun kicked. They teach you how not to shoot so it wont come up. You are supposed to do certain things to catch it and here it had popped me right in the lip.
Well, I'll be darned. Well you had probably got your head down a little more than you were supposed to.
I wasn't doing it right, that's for sure. So they wouldn't take any more chances. They kept me off the rifle range from then on. All I had to do in the Army was march, and all the little things.
But I mean you were promptly sort of put into a military band weren't you?

Yes, yes. But I was really supposed to have been shipped overseas so many times. When I went up into the Reception Center up in Camp Upton I asked where, Clifton Glover was up there before me and he was one of the leaders up there. He met all the recruits coming in. And one day he said he was standing out watching the new guys coming in and he saw me. He'd just got through, and I told you he directed the band at the Apollo Theater, he said, 'Buck, what are you doing in here?' I said, 'I'm in here just like you are.' He says, 'get

out of line."
So I got out of line and he pulled me right out of line and they told me to bring enough clothes for three days. I must have had forty pounds of clothes. I had all kinds of tailor made suits, khaki and khaki shirts and caps and things and I was kind of heavy carrying this. So he made me get out of line.

He told the sergeants up there who I was and so they didn't give me any easy treatment. In fact I think they gave me a lot harder treatment just to see if I could, you know, they called me Jody* from Count Basie's band. You aren't in Basie's band now and you are up here with us and you're in the Army now and all this.

They would make me play a dance, officers dance that got over at three o'clock in the morning and wake me up at five to get up. I'd be the first one they would wake up. See, I'd have to get up no matter how long I'd played at night. I had to get up at five with everybody else. And I only made about twenty-five cents a night. All they gave you was enough money to buy a pack of cigarettes when you played for the soldiers.

But anyway, that is one reason I didn't get shipped to Europe because everytime my name

would come up to be shipped out they would say Buck is not here. He's on pass. He's in New York City somewhere and we don't know where he is. But I'd be there. So they'd scratch me. They scratched about seven times.

And finally when I got a requisition to go to Camp Shanks from Sy Oliver they said, okay, that's good enough. They didn't scratch me from there and I went on over there. I stayed there about a year. Then I went to Camp Kilmer in New Brunswick which was a big camp. Jimmy Crawford was there. Me and Sy both went over there and we had a very good band. A very good band.

But I kind of liked as I said, when everybody was breaking their neck to get out on Friday, sometimes I'd be the only one in the barracks on Sunday because I was just resting from all of that travelling with Basie.

And they used to tell me I was crazy, but I could eat any kind of Army food. I felt sorry for the people who had bad stomaches. I could eat, I didn't care how tough the meat was, I'd eat it and like it. So I used to wear my leggings around. Nobody put on leggings but me. (LAUGHTER).
Well, but how much work, music did you have to play out there, what did you do?
Well, we practiced mostly, most of the time. Sy would make arrangements.
Sy Oliver?

Yes. He was the main arranger and we played on the radio. We had one show once a week where soldiers would come from all different camps. Sy would make arrangements and other people would make arrangements. And we rehearsed and then we'd do this big show every week That was one thing we did. Another thing we did was to play will head That's to play for the soldiers as they are getting on the boat to go to Europe. And we'd sometimes go out there five o'clock in the morning, freezing cold and stay there until two or three o'clock in the afternoon, playing as these soldiers would march up the gang plank. And we played these military songs like 'Lay that Pistol Down, Babe' and we'd play 'Flying Home' and they're going to Europe. And sometimes it would be so cold that the valves on our trumpets would stick, go down. And they'd just make us take them inside
heat them up by the stove, until they got working, bring them back out again until they froze again, and when they froze again go in there and warm them up again, that kind of stuff.

So we would play at all the piers in New York. Every pier that they had soldiers going over. We had to do the same thing when the War was over. We had to stay there and play when they came back. We was the last ones to get out.
When did you get out?
I got out in '46.
Oh, you were there ......
Three years.
The War ended in '45 didn't it?
Yes. I tell you, we had to stay since we didn't go over, they figured we could stay there and play until they got back.
Yes, well.......

And we had ten trumpets in Camp Kilmer, including Sy and myself. We had ten trumpets altogether. And I seemed to be the last one to have joined in '43. I was the last trumpet to get out. And even at that, they tried to make me do it for a retreat parade with one trumpet.

Lots of clarinets and a trombone, but one trumpet. I said, how can I play a parade? So this Warrant Officer he was a scary kind of guy, he didn't want to upset the brass, he says, I don't know, but you've got to do it. So I said, when I get tired I'm just going to take down. If I can't play, you know, I'll play as long as I can. If there were other trumpets playing, nobody always. So he said, well do the best you can.

I played in one retreat parade and they broke up the band the next day. Sounded so bad, 'cause I just quit, I played as much as I could. With no trumpet there's no lead, just a lot of harmony. So they broke up the band the next day, no more. So pretty soon I got out.
But I think you told me once that during the time you were there you were able to get into New York.

Oh yes. I kept, you see, New Brunswick is only 45 minutes from New York. We got through at five o'clock in the evening. I'd be at home around six. Could be in New York six-fifteen, six-thirty. And I kept a room in the Teresa Hotel the whole time I was in the Army. So I would come on in
stay in the Thereat. But if I had to be there six o'clock the next morning then I had to get up early.
How would you get out there?
By train.
Oh, I see.
Or bus. We always took the train.
You didn't have any cars in those days?

No. Nobody drove a car, they might have had one. But I kept this room for the whole time I was in the Army. Although I wasn't supposed, I don't know, I didn't know of any rule that said you couldn't keep a, you know. But I was making more money in the Army than I was playing with Basie, to tell you the truth.
I was writing for a lot of people.
Such as?
Bands like Tommy Dorsey, Harry James, I even made some for Duke. You know, 'Hollywood Hangover'?
Yes. Was that done while you were in the Army?
Yes.
Oh. It's very good.

I made some for Benny Goodman. They were, they were all paying nice, pretty nice. A hundred dollars an arrangement. To me at that time, so if I was making two or three arrangements a week I wasn't paying but 35 dollars a week in my hotel and I never did make that money with Basie.
I was also writing for stock arrangements for BVC, Bregman, Vocco, Cann publishers on Broadway.
So, yes, I didn't realise that you did as much arranging as that. I thought...... that's interesting.
I wrote a lot of stocks and I still was writing for Basie regularly. You know, I would write maybe two a week for Count and I'd write as I said, for these other bands.

You know, this seems to me one of the big differences. I mean, you say you were writing two a week. Well you know what has happened since, what in the last twenty years, you go to hear Basie, I mean they're going to be playing the same program that they were. Maybe one or two
numbers have changed, the same program they were two years ago.
Yes, I know.
Ellington very much the same. I mean they've got, they're rather chained to their, their hits. And I don't know, I think this is really one of the things that is wrong.
I do too.
Record hits of, have just become too darn important.

I think so. I know when Basie was in the Birdland you could almost tell what time it was by listening to the song he was playing because he played the same songs at the same time every night. And he always had other songs he could play.
Now, I don't know right now, I don't get a chance to hear Basie so much so I don't know if you've done the same thing, but ......

Yes, I think, now I don't know whether they're policy is right or wrong in terms of survival because it's hard to argue with them, but you know if you go to hear Duke, you hear, you know, naturally you hear Mood Indigo and Satin Doll. You hear them every night. The same thing
with Basie, you'd hear certain numbers every night. And they make new records but the new things that are made on the records they don't play. They just vanish after they've been recorded.
But in those days they used to play them didn't they?

Yes, sure. But I always thought that Basie never did play some numbers that we were crazy about. He just, he just had a, he said well, I wont take a chance on that. I know they like this. And he'd play the same thing over and over. But he was just afraid to play the newer things.
It's very, it's very hard to know who is right about that. I feel, I mean if they want to say that the business is in bad shape for big bands well maybe this is one of the reasons.
It might be.
I mean, I know if I were not connected with the business, I wouldn't want to go and hear those, you know I wouldn't want to pay money to go hear more or less that same program
three or four times a year.
Yes. No I wouldn't either. Because I didn't like......
Well when was it you were married again?

After my first wife you mean? Well I got my divorce in the Army, while I was in the Army. I got my divorce for, soldiers were getting divorces for fifty dollars. No alimony. But I hadn't seen my wife then for four years. We broke up when I was with Basie. And she went to Detroit and I never did see her any more.

And so when I did get into the Army I took advantage of this thing for fifty dollars for soldiers. , I got divorced in 1946. But actually I had applied for the divorce in 1945 while I was still in the Army, but in California you have to wait a year and a day before it's final.
What was the idea of that?
I don't remember now. I just know that was rule and I just was very glad for it to, I was glad.....
Well I suppose it was really
now for the benefit of the GIs more than the women wasn't it?

I guess so. Sure. But my wife had run off and she was living out in Detroit with somebody. And she didn't have much grounds for asking for alimony. She didn't even apply for it. So all it cost me was fifty dollars.

But after my year and a day was up, the year and a day ended on a Wednesday, I got married Thursday to my wife. (LAUGHTER). I got married the next day to my wife, my present wife and that was twenty-six years ago.
Where had you met her?
My wife now, Pat? I met her on 125th Street when I was living in the Teresa.
She wasn't, was she in show business?
She was not then. She later became a show girl at the Savannah Club in the Village.
Oh.
She worked there about four or five years then she quit that. She quit that when we had our first daughter. But you see, ......
How many children have you got now?
Two.
Steven was....
The other was Candy. Candy and Steven. So as I said, I took her, the first thing I did when I got out of the Army was to join Norman Granz' Jazz at the Philharmonic.
How did that come about?

Well I had known Norman when I was with Basie. I used to know him out in California around Billy Berg's place. He used to give Sunday afternoon jam sessions and he always had me on the sessions and Lester and Nat King Cole.
Oh yes.
Those kind of things. So the first one he ever did, he had made some previously to that up and down the West Coast, but none across Country. He had had Howard McGhee and Jacquet I think and....
Willie Smith.
Willie Smith. So the first one to be cross-Country was only three horns. That was Lester and Coleman Hawkins and myself and Helen

Humes, Kenny Kersey on piano. And we came all the way from Los Angeles to New York. That was the end of it. Then later, he started adding on. He added on the Illinois Jacquet. He added on Rex Stewart, Trummy Young, Roy Eldridge, Coleman. And it ended up being a great big show. But at least we made the first cross, cross Country one.
When I first heard you after the War it seemed to me that you were playing with much more power and range than you did before the War.
With Basie?
Yes.
Well, I think so too.
What would be the cause of that?
Because Basie was always telling me to play in the mute, for one thing.
Ah yes, yes. But I mean, how did the sort of, your experience in the Army contribute in any way?
No, I don't think so because I played that way before I joined Basie.
Ah!

And as soon as I got away from Basie, I played that way again in the Army. Strong. Still in California, I never touched a mute unless it was just for something special. Joined Basie and played the mute. When I left and went into the Army I played like I wanted, loud naturally. So I played the same way with the Jazz Philharmonic.
Well you hadn't sort of made any changes with mouthpiece or.....
Well we continuously did that.
Well I just wondered if there was anything that had really sort of contributed in a big way.

No. Sometimes you get louder horns. That might be possible but I think it mostly was that Basie always wanted me to play like Joe Smith which was in a...... But I had changed playing all the way, I didn't play that way in California, the way I played with Basie. You know, like the mute is still on going to Chicago, many, cup mutes all the time. I played so many cup mutes I wrote a song called "Cup Mute Clayton". Do you remember that?
You made that record with Ike Quebec.
Ike Quebec, yes, "Cup Mute Clayton". (LAUGHTER). I didn't mind playing the cup mute sometimes, but, ......
You didn't want to be typed by it.
No. So I could play like I wanted to on Jazz Philharmonic. In fact the louder the better as far as Norman was concerned.
How long did you stay with that?
Oh, about three years. But that wasn't constant.
What did you do in between?

In between I would play with different guys, different bands. I played with Jimmy Rushing's band for a while. He had a good band, yes. He had myself, Emmett Berry, Dickie Wells, Buddy Tate. Then he had, I don't remember who in the heck we had on the, on the rhythm now, but he had a good band, very good. And we were all writing for the band. Dickie was writing, I was writing. And I played there for, we played up there

for quite a while.
Then, I was also playing in the Embers Club with Joe Bushkin off and on.
Well now, was that the sort of the beginning of that muted trumpet thing with rhythm that Jonah Jones got into to?
In the Embers, yes.
That's where it happened again?

Yes, I had to play soft in there because it was a small, well they would ask you to play softly. I don't care who it was, they eventually, Ralph Watkins did never put it in my contract to play soft, but I would automatically play soft because that's the kind of music that would be affiliated with Joe Bushkin, mute, but not everything.
I could play open without playing loud. But he has had it in the contract, keep your mute in at all times. Other trumpet players, that's been in their contract. But it was never in mine. I could play soft without it.........
Yes, yes. That's really what they want.
Yes, . They didn't ask me to. I don't know, maybe somebody went in there and blowed loud, so from then on they put it in

the contract, please keep a mute in at all...... In fact, they wanted the room so people could talk. People would come in there to sell real estate over their dinner and they would talk. That would bug a lot of people. A lot of people would walk off the stand, and I've seen them do that, get up. Even Art Tatum one time got mad because he couldn't hear the piano, people was talking.
But really that's what they came in there to do, was talk. And not all of them because there were a lot of jazz fans, a lot of jazz fans.

How do you, you know, how do you feel about that thing. It applies even more today I think with some of these rooms in Vegas and some of the big hotels where the music is put in there and it's merely an accompaniment to drinking and talking and they don't want, they don't want you getting up saying to the customers, please be quiet. They don't want that.
Well you know, how do you feel that, do you feel insulted when people talk through your music?
Not unless they are real loud. Some people come in and talk exceptionally

loud, you know. Only then. If people are having a conversation, it's alright. But some people just make so much noise, laughing and hollering that it's no use playing, I don't think. You might as well be off the stand.

Well, I was just thinking of what you were saying about the Embers. You know, it seems to me perfectly valid to hire a musical group to play background music. I mean in the old days they used to have like five piece string groups that would be playing in cafes and restaurants. And there was the clatter of dishes and the people would yak and the music is, I mean it was really like muzak wasn't it really?
But the other thing is, it seems to me that since jazz changed you know, and people got pretensions about playing concerts and everything, this resentment of this sort of thing.

Yes, you can't just be silent.

No, but as I've said, I've seen Ahmad Jamal and Art Tatum, they'd just get up and walk off the stand, because people are talking. I've seen other people do that too. I didn't have a problem unless they were loud and rowdy person.

Oh yes. Turned their backs.
Turned their backs towards them. Now I mean, that's another kind of rudeness in my point of view.
Oh very rude, yes. In other words, you are lucky to be there. You are lucky to listen to me play. No matter if I turn my back on you, that's the attitude they used to have.
Well, I mean that's the
