(LAUGHTER).
That's a total revolution.
Well that's part of the revolution.
That's part of it, yes. Another part is when you come to work in sweatshirts. Because one of the reasons I started playing music was because I told you I admired the way George E. Lee's band...
Was dressed.
They had coal black, charcoal, oxford, what do you call it, black, oxford gray.
Yes.
They had oxford gray coats. Nice cut. They had pearl gray vests and black and white tie and gambler stripe pants and patent
leather shoes. Now they looked so pretty that, you see, in those days all musicians were invited to the best of homes when they'd go on a trip.

Like they were invited to doctors homes, lawyers. Because that's the way they were raised. I mean, you carried yourselves right and you dressed very well. And that's one of the reasons that I wanted to play. And Herschel used to always look so, he was a typical, one of the kinds of musicians I was telling you about. So that's one of the reasons I wanted to be a musician. When it got to Birdland stage, they'd come to work in anything. Sneakers, sweatshirt, it's getting a little better now I think.
Do you think it's turned again?

I think it's getting better. At least they are wearing, they are not as sloppy-looking. The musicians, I don't mean the rock and rollers because I don't know what the hell they wear. They can wear anything. Old floppy hats. But I notice musicians are beginning to dress a little bit more than they did in Birdland.
Well I guess that there will be like a pendulum swing sort of thing.
Yes, yes.
Well of course, then there was, there was the example of the Modern Jazz Quartet which seem to go to another extreme in that period. I mean, they looked like Undertakers. (LAUGHTER).
That's what we used to call them. The Four Undertakers. (LAUGHTER). That's exactly what they looked like. Four undertakers. They played well though.
Yes. When did you first go to Europe?
How did you go?

Well another case like in California. I wanted to come to New York from California, I'd heard so much about it. So now, I'd heard so much about it, England and France and people would come back when I was in the Teresa, like Joe Louis would go there on exhibition boxing tours, he'd say 'Buck, you don't believe it, you've got to go over there and see.' And other people

would tell me. Everybody told me about Paris and London. So I just saved up enough money. No I didn't either. Yes I did. This is the first time. I saved my own money. Me and Earl Hines' drummer, Bishop, Wallace Bishop and another trumpet player which I didn't need, but he and I were close friends. We all saved up enough money.
Stepter
Well was that (Merle Stepter )?
(Merle yes.
Well where does he come from?
Ohio. I don't know where he is now.
Where did you meet, run into him then, in the Army?
Well, no. He, you see, I also during those years when I was working with Joe Bushkin, I had my own band and he was one of the members of the band.
Where did this band play?
Oh, we made tours down to Virginia. We made Washington D.C. We played the Ioward, we played Apollo.
How many pieces were there?
Seven. George Jerry Duvivier was my bass player. Joe Benjamin, after George Duvivier, Joe Benjamin came. Len Davis was my alto and Skip, you know Skip Hall?
Oh on piano?
Yes. He was my piano. We had a nice, that was a nice band too.
Who was the drummer?

Oh, I've forgotten that little boy's name, he was kind of a young kid, I've forgotten his name now. He was Eli Robinson's cousin. And Step was the second trumpet player. In other words, we had three brass and two, two, I must have had about an eight-piece band. Skinny Brown was on tenor sax. He was one of the Savoy Sultans. You remember that old Savoy Sultan, he had played with Pat Jenkins.
They had a good swinging band. But he was a tenor player and Len Davis was the alto player and me and Step and Dickie Harris .....
On trombone?
On trombone. So we always said, we want to go to Europe. Bishop was

having trouble with his wife. She was putting him down. So we all saved up enough money and caught the Isle de France and went over there. But before we went Paradisio has been to New York, he came to New York somewhere down in that time.

And he told us he said if you ever get to France just let me know and I'll arrange something for you. And we always kept that in our minds you know, because we met him at the boat and we played a lot of things for him and Mezzrow was here then, Sidney Bechet Happy Caldwell, Jack Butler, a lot of them.
We all met him at the boat and we made him kind of happy to be in the States, it was his first trip. So he said, if you ever get to Europe and I was learning to speak French at that time,
Where did you learn that?
In New York. Because I knew, I had it in my mind I was going to go to France. I didn't know when.
You went to a school?
Yes. I learned to read it and write it. So when we got or the boat, we had trouble getting Bishop on the boat because he kept

looking for his wife to say goodbye, she didn't say goodbye. And they almost pulled up the gang plank. And when he did get in on the boat he just boo-hooed all over the place, cried because this girl he had met when he was with Earl Hines worked with him in the Grande Terrace and she was working in the Savanah Club with my wife. But she didn't like Bishop no more and he still was inlove with her.

So just as they were about to pull the gang plank up he jumped on it, came on in and we went to France. But we had a nice ride over there. A very nice ride. It was only a four day ride. Not like China because it took me three weeks to ride to China.
What kind of boats did you go to China on then?
(Taiyu Maru?), a Japanese boat.
Did it take three weeks?
Five days to Honolulu, eighteen days to Japan, three more days to China.
Wow!
And I've got a good stomache. I never did get seasick. But I've seen other people
Oh yes, it's terrible.
A lot of times going to France, I'd be the only one in the dining room.
Well you've got a good stomache them.
I did then, I don't know if I have it now or not, I hope so.
You started with a good stomache.

Yes. I still might have a sea stomache, I don't know. But I know that boat used to rock and all I'd just roll with it, I hever would get, I never got dizzy. The only time you get dizzy is drinking that red wine that they keep putting in front of you for dinner. You drink red wine with the dinner, before the dinner and after dinner and then you try to get back to your cabin. Parnassus So anyway, when we got to France, met us and he had hired a tenor player, an alto player and a bass player.
Were they French?
Yes. They were all French. So now that makes us have six. Me and Bish, Step and a tenor and an alto, oh a piano. He had also
Andre Persianny

a piano. So we made a little tour over there and I stayed there about nine months. I was really going to stay about six weeks. But you see, Paris at that time, it wasn't too long after the War was over, '49 the War had just been over and they were still active and whatever we took over there, like we took soap like and cigarettes and things/that, we could get anything we wanted, mostly, you know. Because they were still short on everything.
Yes, yes.

So I stayed nine months. And I learned a lot about Parisan people that are not rich, you know like they didn't have ice boxes so they kept everything out on the window sill. When Christmas time would come if they could afford to buy a goose or turkey they didn't have no place to cook it. They could take it to the bakery and give the guy a little extra change to sneak it in there with the bread.
We used to do that.
Did you?
Yes, but we didn't do it, we you could could have cooked it but actually, we had a baker just
across the street. But you could get a turkey cooked better in those great big ovens than you could in an ordinary one.
Well, I know that's what they did. That's what they did in France. Just sneak it right on in there with the bread and pick them up a couple of hours later.

Everybody took a bath in the bath house because they didn't have, a lot of them didn't have bath tubs. So I was just glad that I was there in all seasons. In the summer when it's hot, nobody is in Paris in the summer time. They go to the mountains or the sea shore.
But I was glad because I learned more about speaking French and things that are not in the book, you know, slang.
Well you were interested in it apart from anything else. But what was the work? What were the work opportunities like?
Oh great.
What sort of things were you doing?
I was playing, I was based in Paris, but I was playing everywhere. I would go

to Switzerland to play with Bill Coleman's band as guest artist. You see when I wasn't playing with my band I played all over Switzerland and made a lot of money. Sometimes they paid me three or four hundred dollars for one night. And I didn't believe them. Me and Bishop would say, gee, they must have made a mistake. They'd pay it to us in Francs and we'd change the Francs the next day and they'd give us three or four hundred dollars in dollars. And we were sure they'd made a mistake but there was just a lot of money.
And in LUZERNE, around we'd play for one big ball. And we were known as the great American artists. Me from Count Basie, Bish from Earl Hines. And they paid us about seven hundred dollars, I think.
Lucerne, Switzerland

Yes, yes. Well, I actually, they could have let me out after the second day but they kept me there to try to figure out why. And they gave me all kinds of tests and they still couldn't find out why. They gave me a liver test and ex-rays and they still never found out.
Well that didn't cost anything did it?
No. They let me out just in time to go to Bern, Switzerland and I got to Bern, Switzerland.
By that time you felt better I guess, eh?

Laying in the hospital just doing nothing, I wasn't bleeding or anything. I was just laying there waiting for dinner time to come. But it was a good rest, you see, so when I got out I flew right to Bern, Switzerland and played at the Chikita Club.

Then I went from Bern to Belgium. From Belgium back to France and from France back home. But I've had, my pressure has been high for years and years and years ago and I don't know when it first started. But anyway, it's normal now but I have to keep it that way, but if I don't do anything it would right back up.
Well what do you............(UNABLE TO HEAR END OF SENTENCE).

Well some of the most important things that I think that I enjoyed mostly was our battle at the Savoy Ballroom. We had quite a few of them up there with all the bands. With Erskine Hawkins, Benny Goodman. But the most things that I
enjoyed was our battle with Lionel Hampton.
Oh.

Yes, you see, they had a a very good band and they had Dexter Gordon, Illinois Jacquet, Marshal Royal, Ernie Royal, the whole band was a good band. One of Lionel's best bands. And they had gotten a little cocky. We knew they had a good band but they were going to do so much to us. We always got the message that Lionel is supposed to do this and do that.
But we had the battle and there wasn't any doubt about who won it and nobody, they would always say Lionel had a very good band, but we won the battle.
Another one was with, a close one was with Chick Webb when he had Ella Fitzgerald when she had just made "A Tiskit a Taskit".
But you were supposed to have won that.
Yes.
Because you know, my wife was doing publicity for Chick Webb at that time and she really engineered that.
Did she?
Yes, because she wanted to prove to Chick you know, that the music could make it at that time. Whereas Chick felt that you'd got Ella and it's best to turn in a more commercial ......

Yes, well we, as I say, we didn't kill ourselves. We actually knew that we won that one and we also won the one against Benny Goodman in Madison Square Garden. And even Benny admitted it. And that's when Benny had a very good band.
What about Lunceford, did you ever come up against that?

We played against Lunceford but it wasn't too much of a battle for some reason. It was way up in Connecticut somewhere and although we played, I don't know, we just figured, to us it was more like just two bands playing.
Well the styles were too different I guess?
I guess so, I guess so, yes. But as I said, the time we did get cut was by Lucky Millinder.
Well that was early on, wasn't it?
That was early on, yes. And we also got cut then, when we first got to New York, Woody Herman.
Oh.

Made us feel like packing up and going back to Kansas City. (LAUGHTER). In the Roseland. We played 'King Porter Stamp'. That was one of our best numbers and they didn't wait until we got through with it. They started in before we got finished and just went on with it and played it so much better than we did that we really wanted to come back home.
Did you ever play a battle with Duke anywhere?
In Kansas City we did.
What, that night during your relief?
Yes. The night we were, Halloween night.
That's the only time you had, I mean, the time you played?
Yes.
Oh, that's too bad.
We were a little raggedy band trying to play against Duke Ellington. We felt we,
we felt like, I guess we felt like Lionel Hampton's band did.
Yes, after you got through with it?

I don't know why because Duke had so much. He had everything, but you listen to some of the guys, 'we can match them, we can out-swing them cats.' Although we just played little old stuff we had which wasn't very much. I, to me now, it wasn't even a battle considering who, all the guys that Duke had, and everything that they were doing in '36. It couldn't have been much of a battle.
Not in '36.
No.
Funny, that was a very, well sort of integrated band at that time. You know, everything was balanced wasn't it?
It was the greatest, yes. It was a beautiful band.
But of course, it depends to some extent on what program, I mean, he elects to play. You know, it's not necessarily going to pull out the swinging things. (LAUGHTER).
Right.
Well how about the relationship between, I mean Basie always had two contrasting tenors. Now were they usually good friends or was there ever ......

Herschel and Lester on the outside you wouldn't think that they liked each other. I remember one time, Herschel got mad at me because he said I was making arrangements with all the solo for Lester. And I said, well look, I said, don't be made at me. I said, Basie asked me to make it like that.

Now he wanted Lester to play all the fast songs and Hershel to play the slow ones, you see. "Blue and Sentimental." But Herschel always wanted to play something else besides that too. So Herschel wouldn't speak to me for about a month. Because he thought that I was making arrangements and putting him, giving the solos to Lester. And he and Lester wasn't speaking to each other. In fact when they sat on the band stand they were on the opposite ends, they still would turn their chairs away from the other two guys in the middle.
Herschel would turn his back and Lester would turn his back. So you got five saxophones, three of

them playing forward and two playing out on the sides. Because they didn't even want to face each other. But they did respect each other as being good tenor players. Although they played different styles.
Herschel couldn't play like Lester and Lester couldn't play like Herschel. But they never, didn't have anything to do with each other. But except that they did respect each other.
Well they, what about the later ones. You know when they had Byas and Lucky Thompson, Buddy Tate and.....
Well, they were no trouble.
They were not, there were no sort of jealousy or.....
No. Just Herschel and Lester. There was no trouble between Buddy, Don........... But sometimes Basie would get certain things in his head. Like he would just want you to play a certain way.
Yes, well I mean he was the leader.
Yes. You had to do it. But it used to kind of burn me sometimes. I would go for
four or five weeks and not play a solo on the stage unless I sneaked a solo in behind somebody that was playing a, singing a song like Helen Humes or Thelma Carpenter.
Now why was this?

Because Basie had programmed everything in such a way, without even thinking who has got the solo, and all the solos would sometimes come out with Harry Edison playing them. So I remember, I said Basie, I says, I says, we've been playing the same concert now for five weeks at the Paramount. I says, I haven't played a thing. I says, I'm not, I might as well be back out in California somewhere.
So that's when he had 'Fiesta in Blue' made.
That wasn't made to fit you.
No, it wasn't. But I think the it might be/reason that he let me play it because Al brilliant had tried it, but he let me keep it. I mean, he made it so that I could play it. Jimmy Mundy's
That was arrangement?
Yes. Then from then on he used to play it all the time. I guess he figured I'd been complaining about not playing anything.

Harry
But everything would be heavy. And so I just finally told him, I says, I might as well be back on the Coast.
Well I don't know. I've seen that happen with other leaders and soloists and I've wondered sometimes whether it was deliberate or whether it's just really not paying any, not giving it any thought.

I think it's not giving it any thought really. Because if he had of he could have split up the numbers. That's the way Herschel was. He used to complain that Lester was playing everything. Which he was, not everything, but he was playing four-fifths of it almost. And Herschel used to complain.
Well actually Lester did get much more attention from the public and critics than Herschel, didn't he?

Yes. But Herschel got quite a bit of attention from playing, from having such a big sound, big tone on the tenor because most tenor players didn't have that big tone. And that is why Lester had been fired out of Fletcher Henderson's band because he didn't have a big tone.
Not like Hawkins had?
And they said, man we can't make it with this cat because....... But you see what happened eventually that light tone became like Stan Getz. And all those guys were disciples of Lester's.
It's strange though because to me, well I mean I don't know what you thought, but it seemed wrong the sound, you know, it didn't seem ......

At first I thought that, but I got so later that I used to admire Lester. But I thought the sound, I always admired his technique and his improvisations. He could do some things I just, were unbelievable. But I always thought when I first heard him, I hadn't heard anybody play tenor. You see, I had been hearing Herschel out on the West Coast. And to me Herschel, Lester sounded more like, kind of like an alto.
Right.
But the more I worked around with him, especially on the Jazz at the Philharmonic, I liked him very well.
Well what did, now what, how did you feel about the sort of changes in trumpet style and sound that bop brought about with you know, with reference to vibrato and tempo?

Oh I didn't like it, I still don't. I mean that's just not my kind of way a trumpet should sound. Maybe today it might be, but not to me. And I still don't like the dead tone, a dead tone, flat. A dead tone. I admire the technique of some of the guys. I admire their technique, but I never did care too much for that hollow dead trumpet tone. And still I don't like too much by (B ?) either.

Well not when it gets sort of sort of sound. But, no everything needs to be in balance. But somebody was talking to me in that Benny Carter band at the Newport Festival and they said that, they said some of the guys in the trombone section were playing with that old-fashioned vibrato. He said, we don't play play that way any more. You can't go that way.
Who was in the trombone section?
Well we don't have to go into

that /but this was interesting to me you know, because they'd all four come out of that same period. There was Tyree, Benny Morton and Dickie. So you know, they were saying well, they've been playing with that old style for vibrato . You can't do that any more. Which I thought was rather funny.
(LAUGHTER).
I don't know who said it.
Well you'd have to think.
But I can imagine.
Yes, well you'll see there's .......(LAUGHTER).
I could tell you three of them that it wasn't, so it has got to be one of them.
Well this was very interesting to me since they are, you know, all out of the same period.
Sure they are. And they are all, they all got vibrato ..........
So one of them has sort of conformed to the contemporary use and the other three have sort of stayed by what they .......
That's exactly the one I'm thinking about. I know who you are talking about.
It is rather funny though. I'm standing there and I'm having to say, well yes I can see where it's difficult . (LAUGHTER).
Well if they wanted it in that kind of band they wouldn't have had Benny Carter there.
No.
You see if they want that kind of band they've got to, well I won't even say that, whose band.
That's right. I mean they were supposed to illustrate a point, the values of the so-called swing era.
I bet the guy who said that must be about 65 years old. He got to be older than I am. (LAUGHTER). I know who you are talking about. Because I definitely know three of them that didn't say it.
Well now, time is running out. Have you any last minute observations to make on your life or on, I mean....
Well, I'm just happy that I've been on the scene for the length of time and I'm more than happy to have worked with so many
Yes.
So many. So very many.
Well I was always very happy that we made that record you know with Coleman Hawkins.
Right.
You know that was nothing to do with me in a sense, but it was just a piece of luck that that came off as well as it did.
Right. Yes, I enjoyed that day too. I enjoyed that day, very much.

But there's one thing about it, I mean you have, you have been recorded; you know we've never mentioned some of the records that I think people still consider classics of the kind. Of their kind, you know those jam session records you made for Columbia.
Oh yes.
You know which?
They were great things that, some of them, most of the early ones we made.
Yes, because they were, you
know to my mind they were much better than the sort of Jazz the Philharmonic jam sessions because there was a certain integrity of style there. You hadn't got, they were not exhibitionistic.
No, no. I tell you I liked them. They were pretty popular in Europe, too.
Yes, yes.
The 'Huckle buck' and all those things. And we had some very good guys on those dates. Very nice guys.
That kind of record can still be made you know. But I don't know how long.
And yes, and another thing, those kind of musicians are getting, more, every day they get more rare, you know what I mean?
Well you know most particularly trumpet players.
Right.
Because naturally the sort of rate of attrition of trumpet players is hardest, but there are very few playing in that idiom now.
Very few.
You know, it's down to.
Sure it is. You can almost
count them on one hand.
You really can. You have Roy Eldridge and Cootie Williams.
Who else?
Where do we go now?
Roy Eldridge and Cootie Williams.
I mean Snookey Young is not, you know, that's a different thing.
I know. Snookey is a good man.
There are people like Doc Cheatham and Money Johnson. But there are very few left. Pat Jenkins.

Yes, I know. Yes, it gets scarce. Very scarce. People like Emmett Berry, Charlie Shavers. Some of them it just didn't seem to me that they are still not here. You know, like as healthy as Red Allen was at the Metropole and as good natured, a good kind of guy he was it just doesn't seem like things like that could happen, but they do. And frankly, I feel great right now, but maybe a couple of years ago I wasn't feeling so
No. Well I mean the thing is that the older you get the longer it takes to recover from any operation or anything like that.
That's right.
Well I think we've just about covered everything and unless there's anything any closing thoughts now.
Well not too many. I was just thinking about my only trip I made to South America.
Oh yes, when was that?

That was about eight years ago. Another good friend of mine, Nick Travis was in the band. Now he, he's gone. This was with Benny Goodman you know. We made a tour of all the Latin Countries and that was something. That was different from everything else.
Yes.
Altogether different.
What did you do mostly? Play one concert in each city or.....
We played two.
Two?
Two. One in the afternoon
and one at night.
And what sort of response did you get?

Very nice. The only thin, when we got there you know they took all our names off the passport, our passports. Well you know, you didn't know who was who. Nobody knew I'm trumpeter Wilbur Clayton. (LAUGHTER). And all of those names nobody knew who in the heck was all these funny names. They just took the whole names off of the passport and put them up on the wall. Somebody was called Mousey Alexander, we found out his name was Elmore. (LAUGHTER?). Elmore Alexander on the drums I worked with Benny in the Waldorf Astoria. That was another hectic thing. Every night he fired somebody.
How long ago was that?
Oh just, just/'72. This must have been about ten years ago.
How do you get along with him personally?
Okay. Yes, but I never know what he's going to do. You never know what, if he

gets mad you don't know what he's mad at. One night he came in the dressing room and we don't know yet why he was mad, he just came in and he was so mad he was red, you know. He worked himself up to something. When he came in he says, I want you guys to listen to me. He says, I'm the boss, I want you to know that. I'm the boss and I want you to play to suit me, don't play to suit yourself

So we didn't know what the heck he was talking about. And he just raved like that for about five minutes. Nobody said a word. He opened the door to go out and walked right into the broom closet. He picked the wrong door and he was, oh boy, we could have killed ourselves with laughing.
(LAUGHTER).
Well I have a feeling that he may be a little mellower now.
I think he is.
Yes. I mean from what I've seen he seems to be more tolerant of other people's .....
Yes, I think so. But somewhere, he'd just been somewhere with Mosey Alexander on drums and he got mad at Mosey and played the whole concert without drums. He told him, you sit on
the side. And that's been in the last two months. He played the concert with no drums just because he was mad.

I know when he was playing at Freedom Land once he'd got Cootie in the band and I went down to hear him and in the intermission I said to Cootie, I said, where's the bass player? He said, oh he fired him last night and forgot to get another one. (LAUGHTER).
He's kind of, you know, I think he's very amusing too. You know, he's got a funny kind of wit.
Yes. He never, he says some funny things to me like he said, Hey Buck....................

segments.chapter: Growing up in Parsons, Kansas
segments.title: Copyright notice and interview header (Reels I and II, Stanley Dance)
segments.summary: Rutgers copyright warning and title page for Buck Clayton's interview by Stanley Dance, with Clayton's corrections entered in green.

segments.chapter: Growing up in Parsons, Kansas
segments.title: Born in Parsons, Kansas, and his musical parents
segments.summary: Clayton gives his birth date and place, says he studied piano from age six, and describes his father (cornet, later a minister) and mother (piano, beauty parlour).

segments.chapter: Growing up in Parsons, Kansas
segments.title: Parsons as a railroad junction town
segments.summary: He describes the town's size and how it centred on the MK&T and Frisco railroads and big railroad yards where his father also worked.

segments.chapter: Growing up in Parsons, Kansas
segments.title: Church life and his father's gospel quartet
segments.summary: Church was central socially; his mother led the choir, his father sang bass in a prize-winning quartet with Wild Bill Davis's father.

segments.chapter: Growing up in Parsons, Kansas
segments.title: Wild Bill Davis and Sir Charles Thompson visit after Shanghai
segments.summary: He recalls Wild Bill Davis growing up near him in Parsons and the young pianists Davis and Sir Charles Thompson coming to his house to play all day when he returned home.

segments.chapter: Growing up in Parsons, Kansas
segments.title: Learning trumpet, the chapel orchestra, and his father's cornet days
segments.summary: He learned trumpet from his father, who taught scales, played in a church chapel orchestra, and had played cornet in Texas in King Oliver's era.

segments.chapter: Growing up in Parsons, Kansas
segments.title: Musicians of the chapel orchestra and Norene Tate
segments.summary: He describes the chapel orchestra's players, pianist Norene Tate, and being scolded by his father for sneaking jazz notes into church songs.

segments.chapter: Growing up in Parsons, Kansas
segments.title: Sir Charles Thompson's minister father and his runaway
segments.summary: Dance and Clayton discuss Charles Thompson's father, a minister in Independence, and how Charles slipped out a window to join a band from Omaha.

segments.chapter: Growing up in Parsons, Kansas
segments.title: First jazz gig at five dollars with four songs
segments.summary: A visiting five-piece band hired Clayton after only a few months on trumpet; he knew four tunes and played them all night.

segments.chapter: Growing up in Parsons, Kansas
segments.title: A band at age eight with piano, drums and combs
segments.summary: He recalls leading a little party band as a child pianist and the pay of a few dollars each.

segments.chapter: Growing up in Parsons, Kansas
segments.title: Records, Bessie Smith and Armstrong's influence
segments.summary: Records of Bessie Smith and Louis Armstrong reached Parsons, but no big names ever came to town, 150 miles from Kansas City.

segments.chapter: Growing up in Parsons, Kansas
segments.title: Touring minstrel and vaudeville shows
segments.summary: He remembers the Billy King and Drake and Walker shows coming through Parsons, his cousin Garbage Rogers, and a friend's mother who ran off with one.

segments.chapter: Growing up in Parsons, Kansas
segments.title: Circus side shows and jazzy travelling shows
segments.summary: Clayton says he always wanted to play in a circus side show, and he and Dance clarify the touring shows with chorus girls and jazz.

segments.chapter: Growing up in Parsons, Kansas
segments.title: George E. Lee's band and Bob Russel's horns: deciding on trumpet
segments.summary: The first named band that impressed him was George E. Lee's, with sharp dress, Cords, and trumpeter Bob Russel's four horns, which made him choose trumpet over piano.

segments.chapter: Growing up in Parsons, Kansas
segments.title: Giving up piano and how it helped his arranging
segments.summary: He stopped playing piano until Kansas City and says piano skill made arranging easy.

segments.chapter: Growing up in Parsons, Kansas
segments.title: Mouse and his Music, his first band, and first Armstrong record
segments.summary: His first band was Mouse Jones's six-piece group playing small towns for five or ten dollars; this is where he first heard Armstrong on record.

segments.chapter: Freight trains and first trips to California
segments.title: Riding a freight train to Los Angeles and a pool hall job
segments.summary: In 1929 he and a friend rode freights to Los Angeles; he worked in a tough pool hall, returned to finish high school, then worked at a rock quarry.

segments.chapter: Freight trains and first trips to California
segments.title: How they rode the freight trains
segments.summary: He describes riding inside, under and on top of freight cars at night, and being locked in a celery car until a Mexican man freed them.

segments.chapter: Freight trains and first trips to California
segments.title: Mistaken for rapists by Texas police
segments.summary: Heading the wrong way into Texas, he and his friend were picked up by police who accused them of rape and took them to a railroad station.

segments.chapter: Freight trains and first trips to California
segments.title: Forced to dance, marched into the country, and escaping
segments.summary: The police made them dance, then a convoy of men followed them out into the country before turning back; they sneaked back to the tracks and he swore off freights.

segments.chapter: Freight trains and first trips to California
segments.title: Getting settled in Los Angeles and California then
segments.summary: A prize fighter friend from Parsons, Charlie Long, got them a hotel and jobs; he calls California beautiful and says he was not yet good enough to play.

segments.chapter: Freight trains and first trips to California
segments.title: Second trip to Los Angeles by bus: Lincoln Theater and Club Alabam
segments.summary: After finishing school he returned by Greyhound and recalls Alton Reid at the Lincoln Theater and Curtis Mosby's Club Alabam.

segments.chapter: Freight trains and first trips to California
segments.title: Trumpeter James Porter and 'King Porter Stomp'
segments.summary: He wonders whether James Porter, a fat little trumpeter in Mosby's band, inspired Jelly Roll Morton's tune.

segments.chapter: Learning the trade in Los Angeles
segments.title: Teaching himself, learning Armstrong and Cootie solos with Pete Kinard
segments.summary: He improvised in his own way, then began learning Armstrong and Cootie solos off records with tenor player Pete Kinard.

segments.chapter: Learning the trade in Los Angeles
segments.title: Growling like Cootie, 'Fiesta in Blue', and other idols
segments.summary: He discusses his growl playing, his surprising Cootie-style solo on 'Fiesta in Blue' with Basie, and his favorites Joe Smith, Armstrong and Cootie.

segments.chapter: Learning the trade in Los Angeles
segments.title: Barber shop job in Boyle Heights and playing weekends
segments.summary: He worked at a barber shop and lived in Boyle Heights while sitting in on Saturday nights, which led to his buddy Duke Ellighew and a taxi dance job.

segments.chapter: Learning the trade in Los Angeles
segments.title: Wrestling in Kansas and why he never boxed
segments.summary: Dance asks about wrestling, and Clayton explains how he did a preliminary bout as a teenager and avoided boxing to protect his lip.

segments.chapter: Learning the trade in Los Angeles
segments.title: Taxi dance band at the Red Mill with Lavern Floyd
segments.summary: His first weekly job was in a taxi dance hall where the band played one chorus per dime; the place burned down after seven or eight months.

segments.chapter: Learning the trade in Los Angeles
segments.title: Joining Charlie Echols's fourteen-piece band; Lawrence Brown question
segments.summary: He joined Echols's big band; Dance and Clayton discuss whether Lawrence Brown played in it.

segments.chapter: Learning the trade in Los Angeles
segments.title: Kid Ory, Mutt Carey and New Orleans musicians in California
segments.summary: He played jobs with Kid Ory, knew Mutt Carey, and explains why many New Orleans musicians who came with King Oliver stayed on the West Coast.

segments.chapter: Learning the trade in Los Angeles
segments.title: The Echols band: first arrangements, Echols throwing his horn
segments.summary: Echols's band was his first to play arrangements; Echols could not read and threw his trumpet in the air, and they played Solomon's dance hall.

segments.chapter: Learning the trade in Los Angeles
segments.title: Earl Dancer forms a studio band; Parker Berry
segments.summary: Former Ethel Waters manager Earl Dancer got movie-studio work and formed his own band, with trombonist Parker Berry doing the arranging.

segments.chapter: Learning the trade in Los Angeles
segments.title: Learning to arrange, Ellington records, and Dancer's gambling
segments.summary: Parker Berry taught him arranging; they played Ellington arrangements, and Dancer gambled away the payroll.

segments.chapter: Learning the trade in Los Angeles
segments.title: Club Ebony, the show, and 'Shine'
segments.summary: The Dancer band played Jack Johnson's Club Ebony for movie stars; his feature was 'Shine' and Bumps Myers was the best-known sideman.

segments.chapter: Learning the trade in Los Angeles
segments.title: Hollywood Barn, the Plantation Club gunmen, and breaking with Dancer
segments.summary: The band played a gay club and a gangster's Plantation Club, where gunmen turned them away because Dancer owed money; they finally gave him up.

segments.chapter: Leading his own band in Los Angeles
segments.title: Elected leader of the Harlem Gentlemen; Paramount and Pantages
segments.summary: The band voted Clayton leader over Jack Bratton; they played the Paramount with the Mills Brothers and the Pantages circuit up the coast.

segments.chapter: Leading his own band in Los Angeles
segments.title: Les Hite's Cotton Club band and Paul Howard's Quality Serenaders
segments.summary: He compares Les Hite's Cotton Club band and its stars with his own, and mentions Paul Howard's earlier band.

segments.chapter: Leading his own band in Los Angeles
segments.title: Meeting Louis Armstrong and learning the half-valve glissando
segments.summary: He went backstage at the Cotton Club and Armstrong showed him how to half-valve and tighten the lips to make the slide effect.

segments.chapter: Leading his own band in Los Angeles
segments.title: Following Armstrong around Los Angeles
segments.summary: He recalls learning from Freddie Jenkins, hanging around Armstrong's hotel, listening to him practice and whistle, and Armstrong remembering those days.

segments.chapter: Leading his own band in Los Angeles
segments.title: Armstrong's California records and Leon Herriford
segments.summary: Dance and Clayton discuss Armstrong's California recordings, the Leon Herriford band, and Armstrong's liking for Guy Lombardo.

segments.chapter: Leading his own band in Los Angeles
segments.title: Irving C. Miller's Brown Skin Models and Frank Sebastian's Cotton Club with Lionel Hampton
segments.summary: His band toured with a revue, then joined Sebastian's Cotton Club, where Lionel Hampton was house drummer and a featured act.

segments.chapter: Leading his own band in Los Angeles
segments.title: What Frank Sebastian's Cotton Club was like
segments.summary: He describes the Culver City building, its movie-star crowd and the big acts including Cab Calloway, the Mills Brothers, Armstrong and Fats Waller.

segments.chapter: Leading his own band in Los Angeles
segments.title: Meeting the dancer Gladys 'Derby' Henderson
segments.summary: While touring, he met Cotton Club dancer Gladys Henderson, nicknamed Derby, and they went together for a long time.

segments.chapter: The China offer, wedding and Shanghai
segments.title: Teddy Weatherford offers the band a Shanghai engagement
segments.summary: Pianist Teddy Weatherford, scouting a band for Shanghai, chose Clayton's over Les Hite's and offered six months at $100 a week per man.

segments.chapter: The China offer, wedding and Shanghai
segments.title: Getting the marriage license and Duke Ellington's plan
segments.summary: Needing to be married to take Derby to China, they applied for a license; it appeared in the paper and Duke Ellington and the chorus girls planned a surprise wedding.

segments.chapter: The China offer, wedding and Shanghai
segments.title: Hesitating by the telephone pole and the wedding at Paramount
segments.summary: Tipped off by Freddie Jenkins, Clayton dithered until his band mates pulled him into a car; he arrived late to a huge Paramount wedding.

segments.chapter: The China offer, wedding and Shanghai
segments.title: Why the marriage ended
segments.summary: He says the first marriage was pushed by the China trip and failed because of temperament and youth.

segments.chapter: The China offer, wedding and Shanghai
segments.title: Sharing a birthday with both wives
segments.summary: Both of his wives were born on November 12th, as was he, and he reflects on the license and the unplanned wedding.

segments.chapter: The China offer, wedding and Shanghai
segments.title: Duke on the boat, the wedding photos and newsreel
segments.summary: Duke Ellington saw them off at the boat and took pictures; Clayton still has the wedding photos, and they discuss the Paramount set.

segments.chapter: The China offer, wedding and Shanghai
segments.title: Two years in China and who went along
segments.summary: They stayed in China from 1934 to 1936; Teddy Buckner, Bumps Myers and Caughey Roberts were among those who went.

segments.chapter: The China offer, wedding and Shanghai
segments.title: Teddy Weatherford compared with Earl Hines and Fats Waller
segments.summary: Clayton and Dance rate pianist Weatherford against Earl Hines and Fats Waller, and note his best days were in the early twenties.

segments.chapter: The China offer, wedding and Shanghai
segments.title: Impressions of Shanghai and the Canidrome ballroom
segments.summary: He calls China probably the best two years of his life and describes playing the Canidrome casino with nightly greyhound racing.

segments.chapter: The China offer, wedding and Shanghai
segments.title: The international settlement, English MCs and cheap tailored uniforms
segments.summary: He recalls the MCs Ursula Preston and her partner, the many uniforms they bought, and the cheap hand tailoring.

segments.chapter: The China offer, wedding and Shanghai
segments.title: Tea dances and light classical concerts
segments.summary: On Sunday afternoons the band played tea dances with light opera such as Ravel's Bolero and Rhapsody in Blue, with Eddie Beal on piano.

segments.chapter: The China offer, wedding and Shanghai
segments.title: The ex-marine's attack at the Canidrome
segments.summary: A drunk ex-marine insulted Clayton with a racist slur and knocked him down; the band jumped off the stand and beat the man while Madame Chiang's party watched.

segments.chapter: The China offer, wedding and Shanghai
segments.title: Aftermath: lawsuit, death threats and leaving the Canidrome
segments.summary: Clayton beat the man, who then sued and lost, but white Southerners threatened to bomb the club, so the band had to leave.

segments.chapter: The China offer, wedding and Shanghai
segments.title: Opening at a new club and Langston Hughes
segments.summary: He soon opened at the Casa Nova club with a publicity line proud of him, and recalls young Langston Hughes visiting.

segments.chapter: The China offer, wedding and Shanghai
segments.title: Madame Sun Yat-sen's dancing lessons
segments.summary: A sister of Madame Chiang came on Saturdays for dance lessons from trombonist Duke Upshaw and testified at the trial.

segments.chapter: The China offer, wedding and Shanghai
segments.title: Half the band goes home; the Casa Nova band and the Five Hot Shots
segments.summary: Worried parents sent money for several band members to leave, so Clayton continued with a small band, and the bassist Reginald Jones stayed behind.

segments.chapter: The China offer, wedding and Shanghai
segments.title: Shanghai night life and after-hours clubs
segments.summary: He describes clubs staying open until daylight with bands, hostesses and plenty of money, while American bands played in hotels.

segments.chapter: The China offer, wedding and Shanghai
segments.title: Japanese soldiers in Shanghai and getting out before the war
segments.summary: He saw Japanese troops drilling in the streets, advised the band to leave, and the war broke out two weeks later, leaving Reginald Jones in a camp.

segments.chapter: The China offer, wedding and Shanghai
segments.title: Public executions of criminals
segments.summary: He describes the beheadings of Chinese convicts at the slaughter grounds, which he never wanted to see.

segments.chapter: The China offer, wedding and Shanghai
segments.title: Food, honey wagons, Valaida Snow's cook and the White Russians
segments.summary: He explains why they avoided Chinese vegetables, ate American food cooked by Teddy Weatherford's cook, and liked the White Russians.

segments.chapter: Back to Los Angeles and joining Basie
segments.title: Back in Los Angeles: a new band with Red Callender and Herschel Evans
segments.summary: At 24 he formed a new big band in Los Angeles, adding Red Callender and Herschel Evans, and returned to the Cotton Club.

segments.chapter: Back to Los Angeles and joining Basie
segments.title: His wife goes to New York and he writes arrangements for Willie Bryant by mail
segments.summary: Derby got a job at the Ubangi Club in New York and arranged for Clayton to write for Willie Bryant's band by mail.

segments.chapter: Back to Los Angeles and joining Basie
segments.title: Arranging in China and the best arrangement, 'Alice Blue Gown'
segments.summary: He wrote constantly for his band; the 'Alice Blue Gown' swing arrangement was considered the best.

segments.chapter: Back to Los Angeles and joining Basie
segments.title: Disbanding and heading east, meeting Basie in Kansas City
segments.summary: Offered a place by Willie Bryant, he disbanded, gave his book to Eddie Beal, and drove east, stopping in Kansas City where he met Basie.

segments.chapter: Back to Los Angeles and joining Basie
segments.title: Seeing his parents again and the young Charles Thompson and Wild Bill Davis
segments.summary: In Kansas City he saw his mother and father for the first time since leaving and heard the young players Charles Thompson and Wild Bill Davis.

segments.chapter: Back to Los Angeles and joining Basie
segments.title: Basie asks him to come east as Lips Page leaves
segments.summary: Basie asked him to join for New York because Lips Page was going out on his own; Clayton found Kansas City a far more swinging town than Los Angeles.

segments.chapter: Back to Los Angeles and joining Basie
segments.title: Reuniting with Evans and Roberts, a month at the Reno Club
segments.summary: Herschel Evans and Caughey Roberts joined him in a nine-piece Basie band at the Reno Club for about a month.

segments.chapter: Back to Los Angeles and joining Basie
segments.title: Battle with Duke the night before leaving and the cold send-off
segments.summary: They played a battle with Duke Ellington the night before leaving, thought they won, and left Kansas City without anyone saying goodbye.

segments.chapter: Back to Los Angeles and joining Basie
segments.title: Pay: two dollars a night at the Reno, thirty-three dollars at the Savoy
segments.summary: After good pay in Shanghai he earned two dollars a night in Kansas City and $33 a week at the Savoy.

segments.chapter: Back to Los Angeles and joining Basie
segments.title: Seeing the country for the first time
segments.summary: He loved touring Pittsburgh, Chicago and the South, having seen only Kansas City and Los Angeles.

segments.chapter: With the Basie band
segments.title: Personnel of the band that left Kansas City
segments.summary: Dance and Clayton list the band, including Lester Young, Herschel, Keyes, Hunt, Jo Jones, Page, and violinist Claude Williams.

segments.chapter: With the Basie band
segments.title: Lester Young as a pleasant surprise
segments.summary: Herschel Evans used to phone the Reno Club so Clayton could hear the band, and told him about Lester, Jones, Page and Lips.

segments.chapter: With the Basie band
segments.title: Joe Keyes's playing and the 'out of tune' review
segments.summary: Keyes was a good swinging lead trumpet on a poor horn; George Simon's Metronome review said the band was out of tune.

segments.chapter: With the Basie band
segments.title: Joe Keyes's decline and death
segments.summary: Keyes later became an alcoholic and was found dead in the Hudson; Clayton also recalls seeing him in Parsons in a Texas band.

segments.chapter: With the Basie band
segments.title: Ed Lewis and Red Nichols
segments.summary: Ed Lewis replaced Keyes, and they wonder why he idolized Red Nichols when most players followed Armstrong or Cootie.

segments.chapter: With the Basie band
segments.title: His three favorite trumpeters and losing a job over growling
segments.summary: His favorites were Cootie, Joe Smith and Louis; he was fired by the Irwin Brothers because he could not growl like their coffee-can player Fats.

segments.chapter: With the Basie band
segments.title: The Irwin Brothers band
segments.summary: He describes the Irwin Brothers band of seven, led by their father, and baritone saxophonist Harris Irwin.

segments.chapter: With the Basie band
segments.title: Why Basie had him play in a cup mute
segments.summary: Basie wanted him in a mute only on record sessions; on the road he played the same solos open in big warehouses.

segments.chapter: With the Basie band
segments.title: Expanding from nine to fourteen pieces in Chicago
segments.summary: At the Grand Terrace the band expanded, but some new men could not read, so Basie replaced them with Dickie Wells and Benny Morton.

segments.chapter: With the Basie band
segments.title: Harry Edison joins after Lucky Millinder's trumpets cut the band
segments.summary: Lucky Millinder's band with three strong trumpets crushed Basie in Baltimore, so Basie reworked the trumpet section and hired Harry Edison.

segments.chapter: With the Basie band
segments.title: Where Harry Edison's style came from
segments.summary: They discuss Edison's individual style and St. Louis background, and the many trumpeters from St. Louis.

segments.chapter: With the Basie band
segments.title: The Grand Terrace show the band couldn't read
segments.summary: The band failed the Grand Terrace show because several men could not read, causing complaints from the other acts.

segments.chapter: With the Basie band
segments.title: Directing the band for acts at the Apollo and quitting unpaid
segments.summary: Basie made Clayton conduct the band for acts at the Apollo, Baltimore and Washington, and he refused to continue because he got blame and no extra pay.

segments.chapter: With the Basie band
segments.title: Earle Warren replaces Roberts; New York union rule and Clifton Glover
segments.summary: Earle Warren replaced Caughey Roberts, and Clayton recalls a union rule requiring local men like Clifton Glover to direct the band.

segments.chapter: With the Basie band
segments.title: Western versus New York bands: rhythm and ballroom
segments.summary: They discuss why western bands swung differently from New York bands, and Dance's theory about ballrooms versus theater shows.

segments.chapter: With the Basie band
segments.title: Differences in soloing and Armstrong as neither Western nor Dixieland
segments.summary: Clayton contrasts New York trumpeters like Taft Jordan with Western players and says Armstrong fit no category.

segments.chapter: With the Basie band
segments.title: Bill Beason's beat versus Jo Jones
segments.summary: Clifton Glover found a substitute drummer could not match Jo Jones's feel, which is why Jo played the shows.

segments.chapter: With the Basie band
segments.title: Moten's band and Kansas City style
segments.summary: They discuss Bennie Moten's early success, the Basie-Rushing-Lips Page band as the real peak, and regional jazz styles.

segments.chapter: With the Basie band
segments.title: His first arrangement for Basie: 'Baby Girl'
segments.summary: He had been arranging since the Reno Club and wrote his first Basie piece, 'Baby Girl', for his niece Jackie.

segments.chapter: With the Basie band
segments.title: The nine-piece Reno band and Buster Smith's departure
segments.summary: Clayton works out the nine-man Reno Club instrumentation and explains that Buster Smith had left for Texas, so Caughey Roberts was brought in.

segments.chapter: With the Basie band
segments.title: The Famous Door and Pittsburgh, John Hammond and Willard Alexander
segments.summary: The band played the tiny Famous Door in New York and the Chatterbox in Pittsburgh, where George Simon and Hammond heard them.

segments.chapter: With the Basie band
segments.title: Billie Holiday and Helen Humes: who came first
segments.summary: Clayton and Dance sort out whether Billie or Helen came first, and recall arranging 'I Can't Get Started' for Billie.

segments.chapter: With the Basie band
segments.title: Helen Humes joins from Cincinnati
segments.summary: Helen Humes was discovered singing in Cincinnati around the time Earle Warren joined, and gambled with the guys on the bus.

segments.chapter: With the Basie band
segments.title: Band feuds and the toll of the road on marriages
segments.summary: He says he avoided band quarrels, and discusses how touring hurt marriages and families.

segments.chapter: With the Basie band
segments.title: Pay and expenses on the road
segments.summary: With $24 a night, work only a few nights a week and two sets of expenses, musicians like him and Harry Edison could barely save.

segments.chapter: With the Basie band
segments.title: After-work habits and drinking
segments.summary: Musicians had nowhere to go after two a.m. but whiskey places, which Clayton and Dance link to alcoholism.

segments.chapter: With the Basie band
segments.title: The 1939 Golden Gate Exposition in San Francisco
segments.summary: The band played ten days outdoors at the San Francisco fair in sharp uniforms, as its records began to sell.

segments.chapter: With the Basie band
segments.title: The band's peak, Herschel's death, movies and hit records
segments.summary: He thinks the band peaked about 1941, recalls Herschel Evans's death, Hollywood pictures, and records such as 'Sent for You Yesterday'.

segments.chapter: With the Basie band
segments.title: The many arrangers in Basie's band
segments.summary: Dance notes the band used many arrangers, including Dickie Wells, Andy Gibson and Buster Harding, yet kept its character.

segments.chapter: With the Basie band
segments.title: Playing Carnegie Hall and his mother's view of jazz
segments.summary: His first Carnegie Hall concert was 'Spirituals to Swing', which finally won his mother over; she hated jazz because of the Yellow Front and drinking deaths.

segments.chapter: Army years
segments.title: Lost draft card and being called up
segments.summary: He and Freddie Greene lost their cards; writing for a new one got him drafted, the first in Basie's band to go.

segments.chapter: Army years
segments.title: Army camps, gaining weight and the rifle that hit his lip
segments.summary: He took the Army as a rest, was in Upton and Shanks, put on thirty pounds, and was kept off the rifle range after a kick hit his mouth.

segments.chapter: Army years
segments.title: Hard treatment as Basie's 'Jody' and avoiding being shipped overseas
segments.summary: Clifton Glover pulled him out of the induction line, sergeants rode him, and he kept being scratched from shipping lists until Sy Oliver requested him.

segments.chapter: Army years
segments.title: Army band duty: shows, piers, retreat parade and discharge
segments.summary: At Camp Kilmer the band played radio shows and sent off troop ships on freezing piers; he was among the last out in 1946 after a one-trumpet retreat parade.

segments.chapter: Army years
segments.title: Keeping a Harlem hotel room and arranging for other bands
segments.summary: He kept a room at the Hotel Theresa, commuted to camp, and earned more writing arrangements for Dorsey, James, Ellington and Goodman.

segments.chapter: Army years
segments.title: Complaint that Basie and Ellington repeat the same hits
segments.summary: They deplore that big bands play the same program every night rather than new material.

segments.chapter: After the Army: JATP, clubs and first Europe trips
segments.title: Divorce, marrying Pat, and their children
segments.summary: His divorce came through in 1946 and he married his present wife Pat the next day; they have two children.

segments.chapter: After the Army: JATP, clubs and first Europe trips
segments.title: Joining Norman Granz's Jazz at the Philharmonic
segments.summary: On leaving the Army he joined JATP and the first cross-country tour with Lester Young, Coleman Hawkins and Helen Humes.

segments.chapter: After the Army: JATP, clubs and first Europe trips
segments.title: Playing louder after Basie and 'Cup Mute Clayton'
segments.summary: He says he played strongly before and after Basie, who kept him muted, and wrote 'Cup Mute Clayton' ironically.

segments.chapter: After the Army: JATP, clubs and first Europe trips
segments.title: JATP years, Jimmy Rushing's band and the Embers
segments.summary: He stayed with JATP about three years and played in Jimmy Rushing's band and the Embers with Joe Bushkin.

segments.chapter: After the Army: JATP, clubs and first Europe trips
segments.title: Playing softly at the Embers and talking audiences
segments.summary: Clayton explains playing soft at the Embers, where patrons talked, and says loud talkers bother him.

segments.chapter: After the Army: JATP, clubs and first Europe trips
segments.title: Bebop musicians ignoring the audience
segments.summary: They agree that turning one's back and not announcing numbers was rude behavior after bop.

segments.chapter: After the Army: JATP, clubs and first Europe trips
segments.title: Dress: George E. Lee's band to sweatshirts and the MJQ
segments.summary: He says he became a musician partly for the dignity of dress and regrets the sloppiness of the Birdland era.

segments.chapter: After the Army: JATP, clubs and first Europe trips
segments.title: Deciding to go to Europe in 1949
segments.summary: After years of hearing about Paris, he saved money to go with drummer Wallace Bishop and trumpeter Merle Stepter.

segments.chapter: After the Army: JATP, clubs and first Europe trips
segments.title: His own seven-piece band in the late 1940s
segments.summary: Clayton describes his small band's tours, personnel including Skip Hall, George Duvivier and Skinny Brown.

segments.chapter: After the Army: JATP, clubs and first Europe trips
segments.title: Panassie's invitation and Bishop's tearful boarding
segments.summary: Panassie had invited them, and Clayton, who learned French in New York, sailed with Bishop weeping over his wife.

segments.chapter: After the Army: JATP, clubs and first Europe trips
segments.title: Ocean crossings and a good stomach
segments.summary: He compares the four-day crossing to France with the three-week voyage to China and says he never got seasick.

segments.chapter: After the Army: JATP, clubs and first Europe trips
segments.title: Nine months in postwar Paris
segments.summary: After Panassie hired a French rhythm section, he stayed nine months, learned about postwar Parisian life and picked up slang.

segments.chapter: After the Army: JATP, clubs and first Europe trips
segments.title: Playing Switzerland for big pay
segments.summary: Based in Paris he guested with Bill Coleman in Switzerland, earning hundreds of dollars a night.

segments.chapter: After the Army: JATP, clubs and first Europe trips
segments.title: Sightseeing in Europe: Joan of Arc, Carcassonne, Stonehenge
segments.summary: He enthuses over historic sites such as Joan of Arc's, Carcassonne and Stonehenge.

segments.chapter: After the Army: JATP, clubs and first Europe trips
segments.title: Switzerland, the Blue Note in Paris, and returning home
segments.summary: He played with Bill Coleman in Bern, did Paris Blue Note with Lil Armstrong and Don Byas, then went home while Bishop stayed.

segments.chapter: After the Army: JATP, clubs and first Europe trips
segments.title: Touring with Mezzrow in 1953
segments.summary: In 1953 he returned for Mezzrow with Big Chief Moore, Taps Miller and Lindy Hop dancers, bringing his wife.

segments.chapter: After the Army: JATP, clubs and first Europe trips
segments.title: Substituting for Armstrong on a Paris record date
segments.summary: When Armstrong couldn't record, Clayton was called with Earl Hines, Barney Bigard and Arvell Shaw for a 1949 session.

segments.chapter: After the Army: JATP, clubs and first Europe trips
segments.title: End of Reel 3 and start of Tape IV
segments.summary: The reel ends and a new tape begins.

segments.chapter: After the Army: JATP, clubs and first Europe trips
segments.title: Touring France and Morocco with Mezzrow
segments.summary: Mezzrow ordered regional food for the band, and Yannick Bruynoghe was road manager on tours of France and Morocco.

segments.chapter: Later tours, illness and the union job
segments.title: Playing the Brussels Fair with Sidney Bechet
segments.summary: Clayton recalls Bechet's fury over 'Royal Garden Blues' in Marseilles and then playing the 1958 Brussels Fair with him, Bechet's last engagement.

segments.chapter: Later tours, illness and the union job
segments.title: Bechet and the microphone; Teddy Buckner's high F
segments.summary: Bechet stayed in front of the microphone, overrode the trumpet, and got furious when Teddy Buckner hit a high F.

segments.chapter: Later tours, illness and the union job
segments.title: Invited to England: tours with Buddy Tate, Dickie Wells and others
segments.summary: Jack Higgins invited him to England, where he first brought his own band, and returned in 1961 with Sir Charles and Jimmy Witherspoon.

segments.chapter: Later tours, illness and the union job
segments.title: The Sir Charles Thompson and Witherspoon fight in Geneva
segments.summary: On the 1961 tour, rivalry between Thompson and Witherspoon led to a brawl in an after-hours club, with Emmett Berry hitting Spoon with a trumpet.

segments.chapter: Later tours, illness and the union job
segments.title: Playing with Humphrey Lyttelton and touring with Big Joe Turner
segments.summary: He enjoyed playing with Lyttelton, made two albums with him, and toured with Joe Turner, trying Newcastle brown ale.

segments.chapter: Later tours, illness and the union job
segments.title: Drinking slivovitch in Yugoslavia with Joe Turner
segments.summary: On a State Department trip with Turner, Armstrong warned him off slivovitch, which they dismissed until they drank it.

segments.chapter: Later tours, illness and the union job
segments.title: Shaky nerves for weeks after slivovitch and rum
segments.summary: Back in London he could barely walk or play for three weeks, with his jaws shaking in Copenhagen.

segments.chapter: Later tours, illness and the union job
segments.title: More dates with Lyttelton and Alex Welsh
segments.summary: He returned a few times to play with Lyttelton and recalls meeting Alex Welsh at Essen.

segments.chapter: Later tours, illness and the union job
segments.title: European audiences versus American ones
segments.summary: Clayton and Dance discuss why European fans are more appreciative, including Ellington's rare visits.

segments.chapter: Later tours, illness and the union job
segments.title: Working clubs in Canada and Chicago with Buddy Tate
segments.summary: Back in the States he played Toronto's Colonial Tavern, Blues Alley and London House, often with Buddy Tate.

segments.chapter: Later tours, illness and the union job
segments.title: Zurich Casabar and the Swiss recording with Henri Chaix
segments.summary: In recent years he played Zurich's Casabar and made 'Swinging the Blues' with Swiss musicians.

segments.chapter: Later tours, illness and the union job
segments.title: Denmark with John Darville and tenor Jesper Thilo
segments.summary: He toured Denmark, played the Montmartre, and praises tenor Jesper Thilo.

segments.chapter: Later tours, illness and the union job
segments.title: Sinus trouble on a French tour and hernia operations
segments.summary: On a tour with Jo Jones, Milt Buckner and T-Bone Walker he lost feeling in his face, went home, and then needed hernia operations.

segments.chapter: Later tours, illness and the union job
segments.title: Time away from the horn and a swollen lip
segments.summary: He tried playing with Jimmy Rushing at the Half Note, but his lip swelled, so he stayed home, and reflects on forty years of playing.

segments.chapter: Later tours, illness and the union job
segments.title: How hard the trumpet is and how to practice coming back
segments.summary: He says the trumpet is the hardest instrument and describes returning with a few minutes of playing at a time.

segments.chapter: Later tours, illness and the union job
segments.title: How the hernia operation affected his playing
segments.summary: He says hernia pain shows up a day later, like carrying too many groceries.

segments.chapter: Later tours, illness and the union job
segments.title: Working at the musicians' union in 1972
segments.summary: His union job in 1972 keeps him among friends instead of idle on Long Island.

segments.chapter: Later tours, illness and the union job
segments.title: Failing a Wall Street physical, high blood pressure, and a hospital stay in England
segments.summary: He failed a Wall Street job physical, discusses hereditary high blood pressure, and a ten-day hospital stay in England before a Bern gig.

segments.chapter: Reflections and closing
segments.title: Band battles: Lionel Hampton, Chick Webb, Goodman, Lunceford
segments.summary: He recalls Basie's victories over Hampton's band, Chick Webb with Ella, and Goodman at Madison Square Garden.

segments.chapter: Reflections and closing
segments.title: Getting cut by Lucky Millinder and Woody Herman
segments.summary: Millinder and Woody Herman cut Basie's band at the Roseland.

segments.chapter: Reflections and closing
segments.title: The Halloween battle with Duke Ellington in Kansas City
segments.summary: Clayton says the raggedy Basie band was outclassed by Duke Ellington's in 1936.

segments.chapter: Reflections and closing
segments.title: Herschel Evans and Lester Young: rivalry and respect
segments.summary: The two tenors would not speak or face each other on stage, but respected one another.

segments.chapter: Reflections and closing
segments.title: Basie's programming and the origin of 'Fiesta in Blue'
segments.summary: Basie's programming left Clayton few solos, until he complained and 'Fiesta in Blue' was assigned to him.

segments.chapter: Reflections and closing
segments.title: Lester's light tone versus Herschel's big sound
segments.summary: They discuss Lester's tone, its influence on later players like Stan Getz, and how Clayton came to admire it.

segments.chapter: Reflections and closing
segments.title: Disliking bop trumpet tone; old-fashioned trombone vibrato
segments.summary: Clayton dislikes the dead bop trumpet tone, and they joke about the trombonists in Benny Carter's Newport band.

segments.chapter: Reflections and closing
segments.title: Closing thoughts and Columbia jam session records
segments.summary: He is happy to have worked with so many players and praises his Columbia jam session records.

segments.chapter: Reflections and closing
segments.title: Fewer and fewer trumpet players left
segments.summary: They lament how few swing trumpeters remain, including Roy Eldridge and Cootie Williams.

segments.chapter: Reflections and closing
segments.title: South American tour with Benny Goodman
segments.summary: He recalls his only South American tour with Goodman, where passports revealed players' real names.

segments.chapter: Reflections and closing
segments.title: Benny Goodman's temper at the Waldorf
segments.summary: Clayton tells stories of Goodman firing musicians nightly, raging in the dressing room, and walking into a closet.

segments.chapter: Reflections and closing
segments.title: Clayton's written corrections
segments.summary: Appended notes Clayton sent in to correct names and details in the transcript.
